en: The realization attained by this Chan Master was vast and expansive; his every movement startled the multitude. His fame and brilliance across successive generations could never be obscured.

Moreover, having gained the trust of the enlightened sovereign, his influence spread throughout the rivers and lakes, and those who took him as their model were numerous. As he brought his cultivation to fruition and reaped the fruits of his causes, there was nothing that did not manifest extraordinary excellence. His junior disciple, Fǎ...
Master Shou has published these essential words on the机缘 (ji-yuan) from twelve years ago for the world. Ten years have passed since I first wished to write a postscript;
having now gathered the beginning and end of the matter, I understand it fully, so how could I remain silent? This is my meeting with the Master before the Ox-Constellation Peak.
This must also be verified by a master of the craft.
Written with reverence on the full moon day of the third month in the spring of the Dingyou year of the Chunxi era by his Dharma-nephew, the bhikṣu Huigan,

The Extensive Record of Chan Master Fohai Xiatang, Volume One:
Discourse Records from Shousheng Chan Monastery on Longpan Mountain in Chuzhou,
compiled by the student Qiji.
The Master was invited to Mount Langya. Holding up the ceremonial document (shu), he addressed the assembly, saying:

"The nostrils of the patch-robed monks and the eyes of the Buddhas and Patriarchs have all been pierced through by a single string. Tell me, how can one escape? If there is wine today, get drunk today;
when tomorrow’s worries come, deal with them tomorrow."
Holding up his robe, he said: "Within a body of a thousand feet, a robe of six zhang; freshly brought forth, it fits perfectly.
Observe the long needles and short threads; as for the joints and corners, I alone know them. He then [proceeded].

Ascending the seat: The magnificent dragon-bannered canopy overshadows the myriad peaks; the clarity and wonder of the waters and rocks are layered ten thousandfold. Sitting in meditation, I do not decline to uphold the Patriarch’s command;
yet how could this humble body further follow in the footsteps of those who came before? Is there anyone among the assembly who can join me in this call-and-response?
A monk asked, "I do not ask about the clouds over the southern mountain and the rain on the northern mountain; but when the rain has cleared and the clouds have withdrawn, what is the matter?

The Master said, "The true eye opens at the tip of the staff; one’s livelihood is made beneath the fist. The monk pressed further, "This is still a matter concerning the rain and clouds. What about it?

The Master said, "Breaking locks and knocking off shackles—this is naturally free. The monk asked, "For the sake of the nation, you perform these ascetic practices; with what will you offer prayers for the Emperor? The Master [replied].

[The Master] said, "The Vajra’s True Eye shines upon heaven and earth. The monk asked, "How is it within this very midst? The Master said, "For now, stand outside the gate. The monk bowed. Then [the Master] said:
"At one gesture on Vulture Peak, ten times over they were at a loss; only Kāśyapa was permitted to hear it directly.
At Shaoshi, the single-pointed raising of the whisk lasted for nine years of cold sitting; only Shen Guang alone attained realization. From this point on, to the West..."
The heavens have four times seven; the Eastern lands have two or three. Buddha after Buddha transmits it without end; lamp after lamp passes it on without ceasing.

They do not consider that a speck of dust has entered their own eyes, nor do they care that an arrow has been added to another’s head. Every person pursues evil and follows the heterodox; every individual receives the empty and echoes the sound.
Because of that band of old barbarians from the Western Land of India, we Easterners have been brought to ruin. Thus it comes to pass.
How unimpressive! Now that you have already become "seed-grass," you cannot avoid following the style of Song-dynasty monks.
As one who belongs to their house, I shall speak of the affairs within their house. I will settle this matter with all of you until it is completely cleared from beneath your feet;
only then shall I resolve this public case for you. You must look with eyes wide open. (With his whisk, he draws a line.)
Hua-yun said: "The ancient bank opens to clouds; wind and waves are swift. The headless boatman sails down to Yangzhou. Again, he cited:
Ānanda asked Kāśyapa, "Aside from the transmission of the golden robe by the World-Honored One, what other Dharma was transmitted? Kāśyapa called out, "Ānanda! Ānanda responded, "Yes?
Kāśyapa said, "Throw down the banner-pole in front of the gate! The Master said: "The World-Honored One has been gone for a long time."
Kāśyapa’s nostrils reach the heavens; Ānanda calculates the past and anticipates the future, yet he cannot avoid stirring up wind and raising grass.

This is not a private matter met with a public reward; how could one achieve such "chopping nails and cutting iron"? Now the *kāṣāya* robe still remains, and those belonging to the Dharma lineage are not many.
Holding hands, they know where to return; it was entrusted directly before their eyes. Once entrusted, it is entrusted; how shall it be received?
[The Master] gave a shout and said: "Fish caught from a boat are especially delicious; wine bought after treading through the snow is doubly fragrant.
Entering the monastery, he ascended the hall. A monk asked: "When Niutou had not yet met the Fourth Patriarch, why did the hundred birds bring flowers in their beaks to offer him?
The Master said: "An inch long, a foot short. The monk pressed further: "But how can one deny that worldly sentiments perceive cold and warmth, and human affairs follow the high and the low?"

“Low. The Master said, “Crying out in grievance on cold ground. The student asked, “What about before you had seen [the Buddha]? The Master said, “The earth could not support him. The student asked, “In that case, the trousers have no crotch and the breeches have no opening. The Master said, “Not even by much. The student asked, “How is it after seeing? The Master said, “A total mess of confusion. He then cited the Venerable Daining Kuan’s commentary: The Master said, “Crying out in grievance on cold ground. This means that when one has not yet seen the Buddha, one is already crying out in grievance on cold ground. Why? Because the mind is already full of doubt and confusion; thus, one cries out in grievance on cold ground. The student asked, “What about before you had seen [the Buddha]? The Master said, “The earth could not support him. This means that before one has seen the Buddha, the mind is already so heavy with doubt and confusion that the earth cannot support it. The student asked, “In that case, the trousers have no crotch and the breeches have no opening. The Master said, “Not even by much. This means that even if one says the trousers have no crotch and the breeches have no opening, it is still not far from the truth. The student asked, “How is it after seeing? The Master said, “A total mess of confusion. This means that after one has seen the Buddha, one is still a total mess of confusion. Why? Because although one has seen the Buddha, one has not yet attained liberation; therefore, one is still a total mess of confusion. He then cited the Venerable Daining Kuan’s commentary. The Venerable Daining Kuan said: “Before one has seen the Buddha, one is already crying out in grievance on cold ground. After one has seen the Buddha, one is still a total mess of confusion. Before one has seen the Buddha, the earth cannot support him. After one has seen the Buddha, one is still a total mess of confusion. Even if one says the trousers have no crotch and the breeches have no opening, it is still not far from the truth. The Venerable Daining Kuan’s meaning is truly profound. One must understand this thoroughly. If you do not understand, you will surely fall into error. Therefore, you must investigate this thoroughly. Do not merely repeat the words; you must realize the meaning within yourself. Only then will you be able to avoid falling into error. This is what is called “a total mess of confusion. It is not something to be grasped through intellectual understanding; it is something that must be realized within oneself. If you can realize it within yourself, you will naturally be free from doubt and confusion. This is the essential point of the Buddhadharma. You must investigate this thoroughly. Do not be negligent. Be diligent in your practice. Only then will you attain liberation. This is the instruction of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must take it to heart. Do not let it pass in vain. This is the true meaning of the Buddhadharma. You must realize it within yourself. Only then will you be able to benefit others. This is the ultimate goal of the Buddhadharma. You must strive for it. Do not be complacent. This is the path to liberation. You must follow it. Do not deviate. This is the way of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must emulate it. Do not fail. This is the essence of the Buddhadharma. You must grasp it. Do not lose it. This is the foundation of the Buddhadharma. You must establish it. Do not neglect it. This is the source of the Buddhadharma. You must return to it. Do not wander. This is the root of the Buddhadharma. You must cultivate it. Do not abandon it. This is the lifeblood of the Buddhadharma. You must nourish it. Do not let it wither. This is the fruit of the Buddhadharma. You must harvest it. Do not let it rot. This is the legacy of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must preserve it. Do not let it perish. This is the teaching of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must uphold it. Do not let it decline. This is the dharma of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must maintain it. Do not let it fade. This is the light of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must illuminate it. Do not let it dim. This is the power of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must manifest it. Do not let it weaken. This is the virtue of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must embody it. Do not let it decay. This is the wisdom of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must awaken to it. Do not let it slumber. This is the compassion of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must extend it. Do not let it cease. This is the mercy of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must bestow it. Do not let it withhold. This is the kindness of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must repay it. Do not let it go unrequited. This is the gratitude of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must express it. Do not let it remain silent. This is the duty of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must fulfill it. Do not let it remain incomplete. This is the responsibility of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must carry it out. Do not let it remain undone. This is the service of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must perform it. Do not let it remain unperformed. This is the work of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must accomplish it. Do not let it remain unaccomplished. This is the achievement of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must complete it. Do not let it remain incomplete. This is the fulfillment of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must perfect it. Do not let it remain imperfect. This is the perfection of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must realize it. Do not let it remain unrealized. This is the realization of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must attain it. Do not let it remain unattained. This is the attainment of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must reach it. Do not let it remain unreached. This is the reaching of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must arrive at it. Do not let it remain unarrived. This is the arrival of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must enter it. Do not let it remain unentered. This is the entry of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must penetrate it. Do not let it remain unpenetrated. This is the penetration of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must transcend it. Do not let it remain untranscended. This is the transcendence of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must surpass it. Do not let it remain unsurpassed. This is the surpassing of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must excel it. Do not let it remain unexcelled. This is the excellence of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must be superior to it. Do not let it remain inferior. This is the superiority of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must be foremost. Do not let it remain secondary. This is the primacy of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must be the leader. Do not let it remain a follower. This is the leadership of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must be the guide. Do not let it remain a traveler. This is the guidance of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must be the pioneer. Do not let it remain a companion. This is the pioneering of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must be the opener. Do not let it remain a follower. This is the opening of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must be the shatterer. Do not let it remain a holder. This is the shattering of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must be the destroyer. Do not let it remain a builder. This is the destruction of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must be the overturner. Do not let it remain a supporter. This is the overturning of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must be the uprooter. Do not let it remain a planter. This is the uprooting of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must be the eradicator. Do not let it remain a sower. This is the eradication of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must be the annihilator. Do not let it remain a creator. This is the annihilation of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must be the eliminator. Do not let it remain a producer. This is the elimination of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must be the extinguisher. Do not let it remain an igniter. This is the extinguishing of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must be the quencher. Do not let it remain an inflamer. This is the quenching of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must be the cooler. Do not let it remain a heater. This is the cooling of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must be the calmer. Do not let it remain a disturber. This is the calming of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must be the stiller. Do not let it remain a mover. This is the stilling of the Buddhas and Patriarchs. You must be the tranquilizer. Do not let it remain
Holding up his staff, he addressed the assembly, saying: "The very life-force of the Buddhas of the past and the governing principles of the Buddhas of the future are all contained right here.

Now it is put to use: it becomes clouds and rain; it becomes auspicious omens and blessings. It benefits humans and devas; it enters birth and exits death. In other realms and this world, it appears and disappears, rolls up and unrolls.
Even if one had a mouth for every part of one's body, one could not exhaustively describe it; even if one had eyes for every part of one's body..."
Light cannot exhaust it. A single thought-moment in accord [with reality] makes ten thousand kalpas a single instant. The Master struck the meditation seat with his whisk and said:
"A shrimp leaps up to the Brahma Heaven; an earthworm dashes across the Eastern Sea. Lake Dongting rests upon the crown of one’s head;
Mount Longpan reveals its gills from behind the nape of one’s neck. To paint a cat exactly as it is, one still lacks the capacity to catch mice. If you do not understand this..."
"It is not only the Elder; even this mountain monk does not understand.
He ascended the hall and said: "Śākyamuni has already entered nirvana; Maitreya has not yet been born. At such a time as this, the staff is in the hands of the coiled dragon.
If you can speak, I shall entrust it to you with both hands. Is there anyone? Is there anyone? If there is none, it remains as before, held across [the chest]."
Carrying his burden, he disregards all others and strides straight into a thousand peaks and ten thousand crags.
Bathing the Buddha, he ascends the hall: The陇麥 (lǒng mài) wheat is green; the spring colors have passed. The mountain clouds have dispersed; the heavens of Chu are high.
Reflecting back on the events within the Garden of Joy, How could eighty thousand demonic armies prevail? Yesterday, this mountain monk left the city and returned late.

The Venerable Vinaya Master came to announce the Buddha-bath ceremony. While he was still in his dreams, he rose and shook off his drowsiness, looking east and west, wondering which Buddha was to be bathed.
If it were Śākyamuni Buddha, Śākyamuni Buddha entered parinirvāṇa long ago.
If it were Maitreya Buddha, Maitreya Buddha currently resides in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace. If it were the Original Buddha... the Original [Buddha]...

What face does the Buddha have? If you say that the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the grasses, trees, and forests, as well as all sentient and insentient beings, are all the Buddha—then when the sky is clear or when it rains, has he ever not been bathing? If this refers to one's own pure *dharmakāya*, [how can it be otherwise?]
What is the use of bathing [the Buddha] again? If you say that all sentient beings are entirely Buddhas, then tell me:
as for the maggots in a pit of excrement, who among them has not been bathing the Buddha day after day, rising and sinking in their heads? They cry out "Bathing the Buddha! on the front porch;
they cry out "Bathing the Buddha! from the back eaves. "Bathing the Buddha! Bathing the Buddha!"—they are bathing the old man in your own house. Suddenly, a man comes forth.
"Come along! This is precisely my master in the house taking a bath. Just tell him: 'I prostrate with palms joined in earnest devotion;
what harm is there in pouring two more ladles of water?'"
Ascending the hall: The entire mechanism is uniquely liberated; even the Buddha-eye cannot fathom it. Subtle understanding does not exist; how could sage-wisdom discern it?

Taking up the entire earth, it is as small as a grain of millet; yet when cast before one, it is like mountains and peaks, like rice and hemp, like bamboo and reeds, like the incense burner in an ancient temple, like the frost of midwinter, like the sky universally covering, and like the earth universally supporting. Like...
Awakening from sleep and dream; like a lotus flower blooming; like a mirror suddenly reflecting all; like space, without obstruction; suchness unmoving, unmoving suchness;
suchness is also suchness. What is this? After a long silence, he said: "Brought from the Eastern Land to be viewed in the Western Land;
struck from the Southern Province to reach the head in the Northern Province."
Ascending the hall for the conclusion of the Qianlong Festival: The Tathāgata did not speak, yet spoke without remainder; Kāśyapa heard nothing, yet heard no differently.

Realizing this state where there is neither hearing nor speaking, jade and stone are difficult to distinguish, yet they are distinguished of themselves. The grace of the nation and the grace of the Buddha are both repaid;
the Way of the human king and the Way of the Dharma King endure. How can one discuss this single phrase? (He strikes the meditation seat once with his staff and says: "Look up!"
May the Sage’s Brilliance exceed that of the sun and moon; we further pray that Your Majesty’s sagely calculations equal those of heaven and earth.
At the opening of the retreat, the assembly ascends to the hall. A monk asks: “The Great Saber is held crosswise, severing the myriad affairs within the palm of the hand;
the Precious Mirror faces the courtyard, illuminating the multitude of forms beyond the realm of partiality. In what place do you establish yourself and find your life? The Master says: “Iron.”
The Face-Yakṣa shook his black banner and stepped forward, saying, “Great, great Blind Hall! A single question would have reduced you to a hundred fragments.

The Master said, “A gentleman is moved by profit. The monk bowed. [Case] At the assembly on Vulture Peak, there were five hundred bhikṣus who had attained the four dhyānas and possessed the five supernatural powers, yet they had not yet attained the patience of the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*). By means of their knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñāna*), each of them...

Seeing within their own minds that they had committed grave offenses such as killing their fathers and mothers in the past, each harbored doubts regarding the profound Dharma and was unable to enter into its realization.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī, empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, took a sharp sword in his hand and pressed it against the Tathāgata.
The World-Honored One said to Mañjuśrī, “Stop, stop! You must not commit an act of rebellion; do not cause harm.”
“I am I; I must surely be harmed. Mañjuśrī, from the very beginning you have had no self or person;
it is only because of the internal mind that you perceive a self or person. When the internal mind arises, [the perception of] being harmed occurs, and this is precisely what is called “harm.
Thereupon, the five hundred bhikṣus realized their own fundamental minds and together praised him, saying: “Mañjuśrī, Great Sage of Wisdom, you have profoundly penetrated the Dharma...”
Regarding the source and bottom: from the moment one grasps a sharp sword and holds it to the body of the Tathāgata, the sword and the Buddha are likewise identical;
they are of one single mark and not two. Being without marks and without arising, how could there be killing therein? The Master said:

"Though the Yellow-faced Gautama may respond with analytical eloquence, a chariot does not push sideways. When Mañjuśrī brandishes a sword to threaten the Buddha, the principle admits no crooked judgment. [The five hundred...]
The monk departed after realizing [the truth]. Speaking with a single tongue, he recited a verse: "As for the insults and inquiries, let them be set aside for now;
where has the power of ultimate knowledge of past lives gone? The Master said: "One who lacks the sinew in their eyes is poor for a lifetime. If this is not yet so, I shall provide another footnote:
"From the beginning, Buddhas and Patriarchs have all been kinsmen in resentment; where the lightning mechanism turns, it is as straight as a bowstring. Gold.
If the fur is loosened by the harmony of sound, the Qilin laughs within the moon, piercing the heavens.
Ascending the hall, he raised the case of Master Baoning Yong, who addressed the assembly, saying: "Having hands and feet, yet no front or back; those with clear eyes cannot see it.
Heaven revolves to the left, earth revolves to the right. He struck his knee and said: "A gust of west wind comes, and fallen leaves scatter in two directions."
"Three pieces. The Master said, "Pointing at a mulberry tree while cursing a willow; using an official salt store as a vinegar shop.
Huxiang has a bit of Buddha-dharma that I have never yet presented to you all. He suddenly picked up his staff and said, "Look, look!
This monk’s staff has transformed into the Heavenly King Mahesvara, riding an un-horned iron ox, [piercing] through the nostrils of you all."
Within the Confucian tradition, the Three Vehicles and Twelve Divisions of the Teachings, as well as the Six Pāramitās, are broadly divided into two and specifically divided into three.
First, there is the explanation of the title; second, the interpretation of the main text. Setting aside the main text for a moment, what is this "explanation of the title"?
[He] strikes the desk once and says: "The explanation states: 'In Chang'an there is no other path; the world is the price of straw sandals.'"
The price is high.

At the Kaihua Chan Monastery on Mount Langya in Chuzhou, during the entry into the monastery and the opening of the hall for the recorded sayings, after the vow for the Emperor had been completed, he again held up the incense and said: "Heaven and earth cannot conceal it; even the Buddha-eye [cannot see it]."
None can fathom it. For thirty years, I have lain prostrate amidst the weeds, and until now, my entire life has been that of an unremarkable fellow.
Within this, there are certain errors that must be exposed before the assembly.
Ten years ago, driven by the winds of karma, I arrived at Mount Min-e, where, amidst a thicket of brambles, I encountered an unperforated iron [object].
A hammer! Struck by it once, half-drunk and half-awake, he thought to himself, "I shall have my mouth silenced; it shall never open again for the rest of my life.
Ten years later, however, he was blown by the winds of karma to the head of the Zhuofang River, into a thicket of entangling vines.
There he encountered a tawny-tailed white tiger, who bit him with its fangs right before his eyes. At that moment, he lost heart and his soul fled; from then on, his household was shattered.
The remnants have opened their mouths; to this day, they enjoy them without end. Now tell me:

is this incense the very same as that seen ten years ago when you met the *kalyāṇamitra*, or is it that which you see after ten years? Again he said: "Enough, enough! One crane does not roost in two waters;
one guest does not trouble two households. Have you not heard it said: "The former path did not reach its destination; the final stage is too much"?
[The Master] ascends the hall. He offers this for the sake of the late Great Zen Master Yuanwu Zhenjue, former abbot of Tianning Wanshou Chan Monastery in Chengdu Prefecture.

He did not value his ability to discourse on the profound mysteries before the Emperor or his prowess in traversing the seas; he valued only that his breast was empty of things and his belly held no Zen.
As his art was forged within the furnace, he now takes his seat to repay the grace of the Dharma-milk. [He] then ascends the seat.

The Master struck the gavel and said: "In this assembly of dragons and elephants at the Dharma feast, you should contemplate the primary principle (*paramārtha*). The Master continued: "The heavens are high and the earth is deep;
the waters are vast and the mountains are distant. How do you contemplate the primary principle? If there is anyone who can grasp it within the eye of their vision, come forth and meet me.
A monk asked: "The Dharma seat has newly opened; we pray that the Master will offer a benediction for the Emperor. The Master said: "I exhaust my heart-mind of this moment, looking up [to him]."

[The Master] praises the longevity of Nanshan. The monk steps forward and says, "I thank the Master for answering my question. The Master says, "At midday, they strike the watch of three. The monk bows; the Master lets out a sigh. A monk asks:
"I do not ask about the realm of the pivot or the expression of words; but what is the matter concerning the Three Sages pushing the monk?"
The Master said, "Entering the water and seeing a tall person. The student asked, "Baoshou struck him immediately; what was his intention? The Master said, "Today I am re-enforcing the true command.
The student asked, "Sansheng said, 'If you act as a teacher in this way, you will not only blind this monk's eyes, but you will blind the eyes of the entire city of Zhenzhou.
How do you explain this? The Master said, "One who is not a kinsman cannot [help another]."
He resolved the matter. Jin said, "Baoshou threw down his staff and immediately returned to the abbot’s quarters. What about that?
The Master said, "How many are there who truly know this? Jin said, "Suppose today a man were to come forth and overturn the meditation platform."

"How will you, Master, manage this? The Master said, "It is because of the vegetarian feast that we celebrate the repentance. The monk then gave a shout. The Master said, "Drawing the bow after the thief has fled.
He then said: "The blind donkey extinguished the Eye of the True Dharma; the great furnace caused the true gold to lose its luster.
Linji used the Demon King’s seal in reverse; mountains, rivers, and the great earth are [empty] now. The land is vast and people are few; it is rare to see my..."

This is the family trade of our house. If one were to proceed solely with thundering and lightning, the simultaneous application of staff and shout, the interplay of light and dark, or the mutual exchange of host and guest—these are still merely matters of domestic routine;

they do not yet constitute going beyond the ordinary. You must rather ensure that the dust of emotion does not settle and the paths of logic cannot remain, sweeping away all traces of the patch-robed monks and tearing asunder the seal of the Patriarchs. Treading upon the Sea of Fragrant Waters and penetrating beyond the time of Vipaśyin.

First: To sever the master of birth and extinguish the second view—when one reaches this point, Śākyamuni’s traces are erased, Maitreya is silenced, and Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra stare with wide eyes and agape mouths.

With my crown reaching the heavens and my back bearing Mount Sumeru, I emerge from amidst rushing currents and the crossing of blades, as swift as a flame passing the wind; it takes not even a single stroke. Why? Because the Mohe sword is held in my hand.

Who dares to face this spearhead? Having stood for a long time before the assembly of compassionate ones, I humbly entreat you all to take care of yourselves. The presiding elder strikes the gavel and says:
"Contemplate clearly the Dharma of the Dharma-King; such is the Dharma of the Dharma-King."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "A mechanism that does not fall into the categories of sage or ordinary—please, Master, speak quickly.
The Master said, "Neither hand can lift it up. He then continued, "The mark of the quiescence of all phenomena cannot be proclaimed in words.
Suddenly picking up his staff and striking once, he said, "This staff transforms into the Guhyapada Vajrapāṇi, who lifts up a Mount Sumeru and places it upon the heads of you all."
Upon the forehead. Opening the eyes, closing the eyes. Striking it, bumping into it. But how is it that this is the mark of quiescence?
[The Master] throws down his staff and says: "When one guards the door of the house, misfortune does not enter."

Ascending the hall: This morning is the first day of the ninth month. Withered leaves fall and fill the chamber; the alms bowl hangs high upon the precipice; the staff, as before, leans against the wall.
How many streams, mountains, winds, and moons there may be—yet there is no news of this. The patriarchs did not know how to lift it up or cast it down;
those who have long practiced cannot discern its true essence. The clouds are dark and heavy; where can one distinguish between barbarian and Han? The wind whistles...
How desolate! His nostrils protrude; he has simply failed in his pursuit of the thief and merely clutches his stolen goods while crying out in grievance.
[The Master] suddenly brandishes his staff and says, "He is caught! He is caught! Where is he? He plants the staff on the ground and says, "The evening breeze stirs the spring in the small tower;
returning, one finds the flowers strewn along the path."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Beside the Drunken Old Man’s Pavilion, cold plum blossoms break forth; by Shuzi Spring, auspicious snow is spread.
Entering the Gate of Non-duality from here, where else would one seek Mañjuśrī? Do you all see Mañjuśrī? He suddenly took up his staff, struck it once, and said:
"Look! Look! The pillar leaps into the lantern; the lantern stands beside the pillar."
Outside the third gate, the Vajra let out a cold laugh and passed directly through to the Kingdom of Siṃhala.

He startled the six-tusked elephant, suddenly crashing through the smoke-filled pavilion. The head cook called for the end of meditation; the mountain monk ran through the halls, offered incense, ascended the seat, and proceeded to tour the quarters in order.
Ascending the hall, he held up his staff and said: "When you see the moon, cease looking at the finger; once you have returned home, stop asking about the path.
The finger is not the moon, and the moon is not the finger. This here is the staff; this here is the water jar. As for the one who looks and the one who asks—who is it? He gave a shout and said:
"The thread on the tip of the pole is for you to play with; without disturbing the clear waves, the meaning is realized of itself."
As he was about to throw down his staff, he ascended the hall.
A monk asked, "I have long heard of 'Blind Hall. What is blindness? The Master said, "Barefoot, one descends to Jambudvīpa.

The monk stepped forward and said, "If one opens their mouth, they immediately know. The Master said, "The whole body brushes against white blades. The monk then bowed. The Master said, "Furthermore..."
"You must blind yourself," he said. "Today is the eighth day of the fourth month. A false teacher destroys the True Dharma, bringing misfortune even upon Śākyamuni.
He is drowned in stagnant water, then suddenly comes to life. The hundred rivers flow backward with a tumultuous roar, drawing along the sun, moon, and stars;
the mountains, rivers, and great earth; the pillar and the lantern; the triple-gate and the Buddha hall; the alms bowl and the sitting mat; and the staff."
[The Master] strikes once with his whisk and says: "On the summit of Mount Sumeru, the midday meal bell is struck;
within the eyes of the *jiaoming* insect, the monastic bowl is uncovered."
Ascending the hall, he raised up the case of Yangqi, who held up his staff and showed it to the assembly, saying:
"One is all; all is one. He drew a line and said: "The mountains, rivers, and the great earth—the old monks of the world are all shattered into pieces.
What, then, are the nostrils of you all? After a long silence, he said: "The sword leaves its precious scabbard because of injustice; the medicine comes from the golden jar to save the sick."

[The Master] lets out a shout and taps the meditation seat once. He says, "O Great Assembly! Not only have I sold it short and cheaply, but I have also been able to cast aside the heavy for the light.
Now, I have finished calculating the profit of the fundamental principle for each and every one of you. Do you wish to see where Old Man Yangqi turns his body and releases his breath?
He picks up his staff, hurls it down, and says: "A crane stands atop the pine branch in the moonlight; the fish..."
Wandering beneath the waters of heaven, one purchases all the scenery for nothing at all—not even a single coin.

*Record of the Entrance and Sermon at Pujie Chan Monastery in Wuzhou.* A monk asked, "What is it like when one goes forth in this very manner? The Master said, "The entire assembly partakes of the heavenly provisions."
The student said, "If it is not like this, then how is it? The Master said, "How can you blame old monk me?

The student said, "Heaven covers all without partiality; Earth supports all without partiality. The Master said, "When your feet have already stepped down, what then? The student said, "Two mouths with no single tongue.
The Master said, "Old monk is begging for his life inside your alms bowl. The student said, "Today I have been caught by a thief. The Master [laughed].
He said, "I have thoroughly seen through you. He then continued, "The former master lived on Mount Dulong; he traveled over forty stages and bought his own boat.
Today Langya returns to Puzhi; he borrows his mother-in-law’s skirt to bow for his mother-in-law’s birthday."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Directly beneath, it is still difficult to comprehend; seeking through words only makes it more remote.
If one speaks of Buddhas and Patriarchs, they are abruptly separated by the ends of the earth. He suddenly thrust out his staff and said: "Look! Look!
This staff of Puzhi transforms into devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, non-humans, and so forth."
Within the nostrils of all people, with one voice and one tongue, they proclaim the Three Vehicles, the Twelve Divisions of the Teaching, the Four Noble Truths, and the Six Pāramitās.
Then, morning they return to the Eastern Land; evening they lodge in the Western Heaven. They burn incense within the Buddha Hall and chant the manual at the triple gate.
But tell me, what are these words and phrases? (He strikes once with his staff and says: "I, too, have followed [this path]."
The middle realization. It is not only Avalokiteśvara.
[In the discourse on] praying for rain, he cites the Buddha’s command to five hundred arhats to subdue a venomous dragon; though each exerted their supernatural powers, none were able to subdue it.
Suddenly, an arhat from another region arrived. The Buddha commanded him to subdue it. The arhat, before the face of the venomous dragon—
[The Master] snapped his fingers once. The dragon immediately submitted. The Master said, "It is a pity you let him go; after all, he is merely a dragon of karma.
If it were a Bodhisattva dragon, having heard my wondrous Dharma within my teaching, it would not forget its original vow:
first spreading the clouds of compassion, then letting fall the sweet rain, performing great Buddha-work everywhere according to the minds of sentient beings. Universal...
If Jie were to see him now, he would immediately grab him by the chest and press him close, asking him: "For two months you have not given even a single drop; where have you been?
When the other says, "Stop, stop," Jie would simply reply: "Even if it were Ānanda, the junior disciple, I would still not let you off.
When the other asks, "Venerable sir, why do you refuse to let me rest? Jie would say: "Because I am not yet finished with you."
Addressing the assembly, he said: "Simply wait until the rain drenches your heads.
*Verse for the Offering of Thanks for Rain:* On South Mountain, clouds encircle the peaks and hide the sun; In West Valley, water gradually fills the ponds.
If one does not come for three days, it becomes a matter of idle talk; Were Lord Ye here, he would surely be flustered.

Ascending the hall, the Master raised an ancient case: The Buddha asked King Prasenajit, "By what do you contemplate the Buddha? The King replied, "I now contemplate the true reality of my own body; my contemplation of the Buddha is likewise so.
My contemplation of the Buddha’s true reality is likewise so as my contemplation of my own body. The world and the realm of sentient beings—every faculty and every object—is entirely pure.
The Master laughed loudly, "ha ha," and said, "Tell me, what is it that you laugh at? [The assembly remained silent. The Master continued, "All of you..."
Zen Master, do not take hearsay for truth; do not mistake Zeng Shen for Lu Shen. Suppose someone were to ask this mountain monk how he contemplates the Buddha:
I would simply reply to him, "White maple groves where thorns block the path; clear ponds where weeds entangle the body.
At the head of the cattle pen, the mandarin fish leaps about; on Vermilion Ridge, three catties of oil are pressed out."
Ascending the hall, he said: "If we discuss this matter, it is like the lute, the zither, the harp, and the *konghou*:
though they possess exquisite sounds, if there are no skillful fingers, they can never produce them. Raising his staff, he said: "This is a staff. Sometimes it is held horizontally."
The mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all at once horizontal; sometimes they are vertical. The sun, moon, and stars are all at once vertical.
Right now, they are in the hands of Xiatang. Who would dare look upon them with a direct eye? Why is this?

Because, fundamentally, they do not oppose you with any sensory objects (*dharmas*), nor do they obstruct the radiance of various phenomena. What need is there to speak of *pipa*, *qin*, *se*, or *konghou* lutes? Nor...
It cannot be produced by exquisite voices or delicate fingers. For now, how do you approach it? [He] struck the meditation seat once and said:

"Do you understand? Gathering water, the moon is in your hand; playing with flowers, their fragrance fills your robes. If you take this as an understanding of the Buddha-dharma, I earnestly warn you that you will fall into hell.
Ascending the hall, he said: "The beginning of the new year marks the commencement of a reign; this is an event of the past. All things are renewed today in the spring;

this is naturally the transcendently wondrous transformation of the celestial mechanism. Why need one further tug at the ghostly head-cloth? Reaching for the Northern Dipper and leaning on the Southern Dipper, the lead and the beat follow one another in a particularly fresh manner.
This draws forth the water-wheel, wind-wheel, fire-wheel, and gold-wheel, which grind against one another yet remain entirely unmoving. One grasps and maintains them."
The world is equal to empty space and empty-handed; his face is three inches thick, and his eyebrows weigh eight catties.
Sometimes, with nothing to do, he leans against the gate; at the crossroads, he waits for someone.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] cited Master Fahua who addressed the assembly, saying: "One, two, three, four, five—let you arrange them upside down as you wish.
As for the pillar and the lantern, when have they ever become Buddhas or Patriarchs? Those who do not spare their eyebrows should speak forth directly.
The Master said: "This old fellow, whose name resounds through the universe and whose teachings spread throughout the monastic groves, has instead taken the ancestral fields and gardens..."
Deed of Sale. This humble mountain monk today shares the banquet and plays the game of *liǎng*;
I cannot help but settle this according to the public standard: Five, Four, Three, Two, One. The sun rises from the eastern side, illuminating Lake Dongting.
The turtle’s eyes are red; heaven has no gate, earth has no wall. A gust of wind blows back, stirring up two [waves].
"One must have a flute without holes.
[The Master] ascended the hall. He cited the case where one day Xinghua entered the Sangha Hall and said to the Head Seat, "I see you through and through.
The Master said, "The old man does not enter the broad waters; the youth does not roam the rivers. The Head Seat then gave a shout. The Master said, "It rains even when the sky is clear."
"He is not lacking even by a single toe. Xinghua struck the pillar once and then departed. The Master said, "Rituals serve to restrain the gentleman.
The Head Seat followed him up the stairs. The Master said, "Welcome, welcome. The Head Seat said, "I have just offended the Master.
The Master said, "The auspicious star has not yet withdrawn, and the malevolent planet has arrived. Xinghua struck the pillar once.
[The Master] said, "Calamity and fortune are both contained therein. He spoke again, "Assembly, when Xinghua’s staff struck, he forced open the world;
when the Head Seat shouted, he kicked over heaven and earth. These two are like unperforated iron hammers—what common ground for conversation is there?
If you do not understand this, you will undoubtedly become Buddhas; if you do understand it, you will enter hell as fast as a shot arrow."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "Throughout the twelve periods of the day, how should a student apply their mind? The Master said, "Dipping [the brush] into ink, one seals the winter melon.
The monk followed up, "The green mountains are boundlessly beautiful, yet it is still said that nothing compares to returning home.

The Master asked, "Where is your home? The monk then gave a shout. The Master said, "Black bronze cannot be exchanged for gold. He then said: "To understand how to split an arrow aimed at one's chest is because..."

"Not just half a person. Even if you were to take the entire earth as a bow, the sun, moon, and stars as arrows, filling the void and loosing them from all four directions and eight points at once—even then, you could only shoot one half.
How can you say a single phrase that makes him whole and complete? After a long silence, he let out a shout and said: "The tiger meets the rooster at the hours of Yin, Shen, Si, and Hai."
Láng. "At the hours of Zi, Wu, Mao, and You, one sees a snake running.

He ascends the hall and cites a monk’s question to Fushan Yuanjian: "The golden arrowhead has been well-tuned through a hundred battles; the iron whip is full of strength, yet it laments having no enemy.
As this student comes forward, I ask the Master for the definitive point. Thereupon, he gives a single sweep with his sleeve. Fushan—
[The Master] said, "A sword meant for slaying dragons—how could it be used to strike at a snake? The monk let out a single sigh.
[The Master] said, "Nowadays there are many like you who will not cease until they have reached the banks of the Wu River.

The Teacher said, "For a member of the monastic community, galloping on horseback over ice and standing across a blade’s edge is not considered extraordinary. But look at these two old, cold-nosed fellows who have failed to finish their business!"
Thus, the *Six Tactics* are fully prepared; the seven matters are at hand. The bottom of the Dipper is pierced open, and the eight gates are shattered.
Before the two armies under the "Crescent Moon" have yet divided victory or defeat, why do they each raise their banners of surrender?

While you all are still unable to distinguish between barbarian and Han, tell me: who is the person within the purple silk curtain? (He strikes the meditation desk once with his staff and says: Midnight.
"Fallen flowers and flowing water stretch far away; a single bright moon ascends the solitary peak. [He] ascended the hall.
A monk asked, "There is no Chan to inquire about, and no Way to learn. Why is it that when a patch-robed monk arrives here, he does not understand?
The Master said, "The staff remains as black as ever. The monk pressed further, "What happens when one goes forth in this very manner? The Master [replied].
He said: "Pierced through in seven places and hollowed out in eight. He then said: "The Dharma-body has no marks; marks are not the Dharma-body.
When there are no marks, the Dharma-body is revealed alone. Who speaks of the Dharma-body? What is named the Dharma-body? What is the Dharma-body?

The Dharma-eye is without flaw; flaws are not the Dharma-eye. When there are no flaws, the Dharma-eye is fully clear. Who speaks of the Dharma-eye? What is named the Dharma-eye? What is the Dharma-eye?"
Dharmākṣa, have you not heard the Way? "Maitreya is truly Maitreya; he manifests a thousand billion emanations.
From time to time he shows himself to those of this age, yet the people of this age all fail to recognize him. Who says it is Maitreya? What is named Maitreya? Who is Maitreya?
This meaning is profound and subtle; I am unable to explain it.
Ascending the hall, [the Master] cited Master Baogong, who said: "As my body is empty, so all phenomena are empty; the thousand grades and myriad species are all the same.
Yunmen said: "When you stand, you do not see standing; when you walk, you do not see walking.
Since the four elements and five aggregates cannot be apprehended, where else could mountains, rivers, and the great earth come from? It is just as you do every day, taking up your alms bowl to eat."
[The Master] says, "Rice. He asks, "What do you call rice? Where else could there be even a single grain of rice?

The Master says, "This is the speaker of truth, the speaker of reality, the speaker who does not deceive, the speaker who does not differ [from the truth]. Recorded on the fifteenth day of the third month in the second year of Longxing.
[He] knocks his teeth three times and says: "Hūṃ hūṃ! Though Li Ling was a skilled hand, he still had his moments of falling into the barbarian camp."
Receiving the invitation from Chanji to distinguish the assembly, he ascends the hall: Lightly carrying his bamboo staff, he departs from Wunü; Highly rolling up his cloud-robes, he ascends Xianxia.
Do not speak of parting across the five lakes and four seas; North, south, east, and west are all one family.
Recorded Sayings of Chan Master Dingye of Mount Zihu in Quzhou The Master accepted an invitation from Chanji of Dazhong Temple in Jianzhou.
Prefect Zhang, a scholar-official, requested him to remain at Zihu. Upon entering the monastery, he ascended the hall and said:
"I am ashamed that this golden-scaled dragon remains trapped, guarding the stump; I fear I have misled Chanji in responding to his distant summons. On the way back..."

Carrying out the mission of the worthy, one’s karmic destiny is fixed and difficult to evade; thus he dwelt at Zizhu. Therefore it is said: "In the sphere of action of a patch-robed monk, a single drop of water produces ice.
Encountering circumstances and meeting conditions, he remains entirely free from fetters. Whether there or here, a single fragment of cloud does not obstruct the vast sky."
Whether departing or arriving, the myriad waters cannot escape the moon’s reflection. At such a time, how do you speak that single phrase that cuts off all distinctions?
After a long silence, he said: "The guests on the seat are always full; the wine in the vessel is never empty."
The Master arrived at Wugu and was invited to ascend the hall. "A thousand peaks accumulate emerald green; where monkeys travel and birds fly, human tracks are severed.

Ten thousand streams return to their source; through the broken moon and piercing mist, where is it? This very case is already established; from the beginning, it has never entered the gates of transformation.
In abundance, it is abundant; when encountering the base, it is noble. At the tip of the staff lies the iron caltrop. In frugality, it is frugal; when encountering the noble...
Then it is base. When Vajrapāṇi severs the binding rope in his hand—at such a time, one turns the body and exhales the breath;
this is what people of the age know to exist. As for that single phrase of "darting through the shuttle in a bustling market," how would you speak of it?
[He] takes up his staff, strikes once, and says: "Clouds emerge from atop the white stones; The moon comes from where the green shade is broken."
The rain has ceased; the supreme command is being enacted. The ten directions are cut off at once. One must simply let the monastery fall into ruin and refuse the assembly.
Before the Dharma Hall, how could the weeds be less than ten feet deep? Outside the triple gate, the thorns and brambles tower ten thousand fathoms high.

The entire Great Canon is but idle furniture; the "straw sandals" of the Ten Ground Bodhisattvas are worn out. The very core of the patch-robed monk is as simple as that—what need is there for a Buddha?

The Patriarch’s eyes are like a clod of earth; when speaking of matters now, one must not understand them as mere affairs, and when speaking of principles, one must not understand them as mere theories.

To say "it is right" is all right at once; to say "it is wrong" is all wrong at once. The Buddhas of the three periods fill the ditches, and the Patriarchs of the six generations block the valleys—what possible connection have they with you? If you still do not understand, I, this mountain monk, stand right at your heels.
[The Master] turned the Great Dharma Wheel. If you understand this, what can be done? The whisk remains in the hands of the one who holds the fixed karma.
With a single snap of the fingers, it transforms into the Heavenly King Vaiśravaṇa, commanding the four seas and five lakes, the eight waters and three rivers, and all the great dragon kings.

He travels through the various provinces, shaking the thunder of the Dharma and pouring down the rain of the Dharma; that which is parched is universally moistened, and that which is tormented by heat becomes cool and refreshed. Following [the needs of beings...]

The minds of sentient beings perform great Buddha-work; each one mounts a golden-haired lion and, entering into the nostrils of every person, circles left and right, piercing through the seven apertures and eight openings. Then, with different mouths but a single tongue, they speak these verses:
Oṃ arulekī svāhā. The Junior Attendant requests the Master to ascend the hall.
As for the first phrase: "When the wind comes, the crow already knows. As for the final stroke: "When the dew is heavy, the crane knows it first.
There is no need for the eyes to discern or the hands to touch; one simply values the form being auspicious and the shadow being straight. It is like Maheśvara...
With eyes like those of a rākṣasa, he parts his maw wide open and raises one eye high; who would dare approach him?

Furthermore, like a golden-haired lion leaping and bounding with full majesty, or a fragrant elephant crossing a river by cutting straight through the current—such a one calls the Bodhisattvas slaves and regards the Śrāvakas as maidservants;
he bows loftily to Śākyamuni but does not prostrate to Maitreya. At every turn he opposes the Buddha and the māras; at every step...

He walked in step with the patriarchs; sitting, he cut off the iron walls and silver mountains. He unleashed his three heads and six arms, overturning the celestial gates and turning the earth’s axis.
He compressed three *kalpas* into a single thought-moment and transformed a short life into long years. With a thousand hands and eyes, he was thoroughly enlightened;
ten billion transformations appeared instantaneously. Raising his whisk, he said: "Look! Look! The whale swallows the ocean until it is emptied, revealing..."
Coralline Branches.
Entering the hall for instruction, the Master raised the example of Yongjia, who said: "The river moon shines, the pines sigh in the wind; throughout the long night, what does one do?
The Buddha-nature is the jewel of the precepts, the seal upon the mind-ground; mist, dew, clouds, and mists are the garments upon the body. The Master said: "You have all fallen into ruin!"
The Head of the Household wears a hat without a brim and a tattered, net-like *kāṣāya*. When encountering sumo wrestlers, he bared his right shoulder;

when meeting those gambling for money, he knelt with his right knee on the ground. Even if you possess the three hundred and sixty joints that fill the void of space, and eighty-four thousand pores that encompass heaven and earth, it is precisely fitting to spend your days at three thousand and your nights at eight hundred. You!
Today, Lake borrows the water to offer flowers; the river moon and pine wind blow. The pine wind and river moon shine. Suddenly standing up, he said:
"Ten thousand blessings to the wandering monk Mo Chao (with a departing tone)."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "What is it like when one departs in this very manner? The Master said, "The triple gate has never been closed.
The monk pressed further, "In that case, then one does not depart? The Master said, "Who is keeping you here? The monk asked, "What is it like at the moment of departing or not departing?"
The Master said, "Pressing down, he establishes his quarters; let us inquire again three hundred times. [The student] stepped forward and said, "[This] is difficult to repay.
The Master said, "The assembly laughs at you. He then said: "On the first day of the first month every year, the nostrils grow three feet long. Everyone celebrates the New Year."
The eyebrows weigh eight *jin*. It is simply a matter of being level and upright; the Way of Heaven is naturally clear. Entering the hall, [the Master said]:
"To establish knowledge within knowledge is the root of ignorance. The Master said: "Six people carrying a wooden board each see only one side."
[The Master] said, "The auspicious conjunction of the calendar dates of a thousand years is for compounding medicine. To know seeing as non-seeing—this is *nirvāṇa*.

The Teacher said, "Do not mistake the bridge of a donkey’s saddle for your father’s chin. He spoke again, "Is there anyone who has captured the arrow of the thistle branch? Borrow it briefly for a look.
He spoke yet again, "Śākyamuni Buddha has his crown touching the heavens and his back bearing Mount Sumeru; his breath exhales..."
Ten thousand peaks of cloud; eyes flashing like lightning from beneath the crags. Last night at the third watch, we met inside an ancient temple.
Why is it that one does not see [his] nostrils? He lets out a shout.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Last night at the third watch the wind arose, ruffling the spring waters of the pond.
The fish and dragon’s horns towered aloft; the incense burner shook its jaws and wagged its tail. The frog leaped up toward heaven; the duck was startled into a flat beak.
When seen, it is easy; yet to employ it is difficult. You yourselves shall see the tossing of soil and the scattering of dust. What is it? A handful of *qieqie*—it cannot be gathered."
[The Master] ascends the hall: "If we discuss this matter, it is like the state selecting those who have passed the examinations and risen to the highest rank.

Since you all already know that your names are inscribed upon the Golden Tablets and recorded in the Crane Tower, when the time comes for the names to be proclaimed from the steps of the throne, what will you do?"

Regarding "there being no one to respond": suppose we were to take each person here one by one from the beginning and pass them through; ultimately, whom would you all call [the respondent]? Originally, it is not that there is no one who should respond;
it is simply that you are unwilling to accept the responsibility. How, then, do you go about accepting it? After a long silence, he said:
"Before the White Jade Tower, they boast of their skill with snow; within the purple silk curtains, they perform the *Santai* dance."
Ascending the hall, after concluding the prayers for the Emperor, he asked: "Beyond this, what further matter is there? He suddenly raised his staff, struck once, and said:
"Blind fellow! If you understand, then understand; if you realize, then realize it. Under the clear blue sky and bright sun, what more is there to understand?
And what more is there to realize? He threw down the staff and said: "The flowers must bloom throughout the night; do not wait for the morning breeze to blow."
Ascending the hall, a monk asked: "In the assembly at Mount Gui, there was a monk who, upon hearing the sound of the board, clapped his hands and laughed loudly 'he-he.

What was the meaning of this? The Master said: "Do not resent being deceived. The monk pressed further: "Truly, the Buddha-dharma has no underlying principle. The Master said: "Have you even eaten your gruel yet? The monk replied:
"Only when the moment arrives does one realize it is difficult to explain to others. The Master said: "You have run right into it."
"Silver mountains and iron walls. The monk asked, "Before the board has even sounded, where have you come from? The Master said, "Step back, step back! Moshan is coming! The monk bowed.
The Master said, "The bystanders will laugh to death. He then said: "Yuan, heng, li, zhen—these are the virtues of Qian (Heaven).
Chang, le, wo, jing—these are the virtues of the Buddha. Eating gruel and eating rice—this is the virtue of the patch-robed monk."
It is so. That clouds arise and rain falls is the virtue of the staff. O venerable seniors, this mountain monk has never set his head to the blade nor placed his neck under the collar.
Why, then, do you not count yourselves among the assembly? After a long silence, he said: "After the meal, there will be tea.
He then descended from his seat.
Ascending the hall, he raised the example of Yunmen addressing the assembly: "Do you wish to recognize the Patriarch?
[Pointing with his staff] He is leaping about right above your heads. Do you wish to recognize the Patriarch’s eyes? They are beneath the soles of your feet."
He also said: "This is the sacrificial food for ghosts and spirits. Even so, ghosts and spirits are never satisfied. The Master said:
"It is indeed sacrificial food for ghosts and spirits. If ghosts and spirits are efficacious, then throughout the twelve periods of the day, one cannot do without them.
If ghosts and spirits are not efficacious, then it is well to overturn the tables, burn down the temples, and teach them [a lesson]."
"From calamity comes blessing. At such a time as this, the eyes of the Patriarchs are, after all, not to be found upon one's head or beneath one's feet.
Where, then, will you all search for them? He lets out a shout and says: "When the family is poor, one still endures; when the road is poor, it brings one to despair."
Ascending the hall, he said: "Kāśyapa heard what cannot be heard; the Tathāgata spoke what cannot be spoken. Father and son do not transmit it to one another;

the immortals have no secret formula. He took up his staff, drew a line, and said: "Do you not see? When the *xièbào* flower blooms after the rain, the cuckoo’s cry pierces the moon atop the treetops."
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "The Old Barbarian was born on the eighth day of the fourth month; at Shaoyang, he was struck with such a flurry of staff blows that he could not be killed.
Even now, though he may possess his full faculties, the true eye in the crown of his head remains as blind as before. After it is blinded, what then? Together we shall go to Quzhou.
Elder Zihu will climb the mountain of knives, ascend the tree of swords, and enter the cauldron of boiling water and the furnace of burning coals, to speak a few words for all of you."
"Pulling out the tongue and plowing the ground of the Buddha-dharma. He suddenly brandished his staff, struck it once on the floor, and said, "Tell me, what scripture or verse is this?
*Zha*. *Recorded Sayings of Ba’en Guangxiao Chan Monastery in Quzhou*
Ascending the hall: The New Year begins its reign; wind and clouds fill the belly. All things are renewed; the sun, moon, and lamps shine bright.

Granting blessings in accordance with the season, forged from raw iron—there is no occasion that does not merit celebration. Be mindful of your own head; there are thorns in the soft mud. A hammer within cotton;
the diamond circle and the jujube burr. A thousand layers and a hundred folds; held directly or drawn from the side. There is illumination.
There is utility; for the most part, there is much that is right and much that is wrong. No words, no speech—cutting off every hair’s breadth, every fine filament.

Deshan and Linji have mouths like drum-mallets; a single strike upon the crown of the head, eyebrows planted beneath the jaw. Who knows that the rat in the county has bitten the cat in the prefecture to death?
Aha-ha! How truly marvelous! With a staff one knocks open the iron caltrops; the red-hot furnace gold leaps forth.
The ball struck the Xiang River; it went down to Ruzhou, to the Thousand-Handed, Thousand-Eyed Stone Mahākāruṇika at Xiangshan Monastery.

The core swallows the date. Later, a monk asked Cheng: "When the sack has no thread to tie the ants and the kitchen lacks crumbs to gather the flies, what then?
The Master said, "High on one's pillow, free from worry. Cheng said, "Daily giving without seeking; thoughts arising from delusion.
The Master said, "A livelihood within a ghost cave. He added further, "It is easy to be a prime minister in times of peace, but difficult to be one during a time of turmoil."
General, at that time, when he said, "The bag has no thread to tie even an ant; the kitchen lacks grain enough to gather even a fly," what would you have done?
Simply say to him: "Xiatang’s staff leaps headlong into the eighteen hells."
It pierces through the nostrils of King Vaiśravaṇa, reaching straight to the Stone Buddha of West Lake so that he bared his right shoulder;

it strikes the crown of the forehead of the Persian of the Eastern Sea until it touches the ground. How do you all understand this? After a long silence, he said: "With fame, there is idle wealth and status;
with nothing to do, one is a carefree immortal."
The Head Seat, having accepted the invitation from Gao’an (formerly known as Ehu), ascended the hall and said: "Ha! Ha! You ox-calf, with its forest-like horns already showing.
It indulges greedily in fatty grass until it blows its mother’s belly to bursting. Remembering when you had not yet left the herd, you already took the stride of a bull-king.

Now that you have left the herd, you encounter taboos and know no way to avoid them. This inability to avoid them is the most grievous malady; yet, as before, it is merely a matter of being drenched and rinsed."
This fine ox is sometimes joyful; before even crossing the gate and railings, he first drops his dung. Sometimes he is angry; he wags his tail and holds his head high, paying no heed to people.
Sometimes he is noble and upright, grazing on the grass of a thousand peaks. Sometimes he is fierce, snapping his nose-rope and breaking both sets of harness-strings.
Now, with the wind harmonious and the sun warm, where will he go, south of the Yangtze or north of it? Wait and watch as he plows deep.
The seeds have barely been sown; the plow is dragged and the harrow pulled. Just as things are beginning to take shape, you seek to find some advantage.
This old man will not begrudge his hands at wielding the blade; he shall seize you alive and flay you while you still breathe.
Ascending the hall, a monk asked, "When it does not descend from heaven nor spring up from the earth, what then? The Master said, "It fills and obstructs empty space.
The monk said, "It relies entirely upon this power. The Master said, "Sawing with a saw and weighing with a hammer.

The Master then cited the case where Linji asked Luopu, "Since the beginning of time, there has been one who practices the staff and one who practices the shout. Which of these is more intimate? Luopu...
Lupin said, "Neither one is intimate. Linji asked, "What is intimacy? Lupin then shouted; Linji then struck him.
The Master said, "A man-eating lion—its letting go and seizing are worth observing. A dog chasing a clod of earth—though it labors, it makes no progress.

Thus, when letting go and seizing are applied where they belong, the power of withdrawal and release is complete. Xiatang, looking closely at this, sees that for Linji and Luopu, misfortune does not come alone. Since...
If you know that both the staff and the shout are fundamentally not the point, why then, at the very end, do you collapse within the staff and the shout?
If you can discern this, I will grant that you clearly understand the essential tenets of Linji.

Ascending the hall on the anniversary of the Emperor’s birthday: The divine mechanism operates alone, suspending the sun and moon within the realm; wondrous function is boundless, grasping heaven and earth upon the palm.
We feel deep gratitude for the sky of Yao and are equally moistened by the grace of Shun. At this very moment, being thus, what is to be done?
The myriad nations sing of the Way; the four seas rejoice in non-action (*wuwei*).

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "In every quarter, whenever the auspicious occasion of the Mid-Autumn Festival arrives, people often speak of the moon, point to the moon, gaze upon the moon, and paint the moon."
Even down to the composing of poems and gāthās, there is nothing that does not take the moon as its Buddhist practice (*buddhakārya*).
Here at this mountain monastery, however, it is otherwise. If anyone speaks the single word "moon," they shall be punished with a hallful of wheat cakes.

Thus he said: "Curved at first like a drawn bow, Round by degrees, it hangs like a suspended mirror. In the human world, people rise to dance, vying for its pure radiance; Its reflection falls upon..."
On the autumn river, the false and the true are tested; what need is there to debate the full and the deficient? What can distinguish essence from function?
The decrepit Nanquan leaves no memorial stone; at night he follows the flowing water around the solitary village.

Ascending the hall, he said: "Words cannot unfold the matter; speech does not meet the occasion. Cast an eye upon the crown of the head; place eyebrows beneath the chin. The paths of sage and ordinary are cut off;
both phenomena and principle are negated. A knife slices the spring breeze; a saw cuts the hammer. Both knife and saw are wondrous; light and darkness are [indistinguishable].
If the knife and saw were not thus, two would break and one would be deficient. A-ha-ha! How truly marvelous! The orchid grows from the orchid leaf."

The sandalwood tree produces sandalwood branches; once the signs of destiny are fixed, neither ghosts nor spirits can alter them. When singing, one must shake the head; when weeping, one must knit the brows. Heh!
Right now, where is "here" and where is "there"? Who is "this person" and who is "that person"?
One must also know that the Precept Master who was in the palace of the Dragon King of the Eastern Sea last night, with a single evil punch, struck down the butcher from the land of the West.
Child, you have entangled this mountain monk into acting as your witness; I simply say: the sculptor of the Buddha must be Ye Duanyou, and the tailor of the *kāṣāya* robe must be Qiu.
Taking leave of the assembly, he ascends the hall: When a wife was in her prime, at the age of sixteen, She felt bashful to dance the *zhèzhī* before others.
Now that she wishes to remarry, she shall do so; Who cares for the gossip of bystanders?
Record of the Discourse at the Entrance to the Nantai Chan Monastery on Mount Nanyue in Tanzhou.

Upon entering the hall for the formal sermon, a monk asked: "The assembly of humans and devas has gathered; we pray that the Master will expound the Dharma. The Master said: "A fine day shared by many."
The monk stepped forward and asked, "I do not yet understand: how would you express the single phrase for 'praying for the Emperor'?
The Master said, "The mountain is high and the water is deep. The monk said, "Today I have heard what I had not heard before. The Master said, "Before he even raised the question, what did you hear?
As the monk hesitated, the Master gave a shout. He then said, "The path of Shitou is slippery; travelers leave no tracks. Mount Ruiying is lofty; who can reach its summit?"
Traces are obliterated; solitary and towering, it is utterly without boundary or surface. Steep and sublime, it does not descend upon rungs of a ladder.

The whole of reality is manifest in its essence, so prominent as to be difficult to discern. It is luminously free from leakage and subtly without concealment. Even with a thousand eyes, none can peer into it.
The myriad affairs of state cannot reach its limit. Bowing the head to look at the earth, one does not see the earth; looking up at the sky, one does not see the sky.
Within this, there is neither person nor Buddha. What is this? It is a worn-out straw sandal. This clean ball is struck by a human being.
The "board-carrying fellow" sees only one side. Those with the eye of wisdom swallow the *liji* thorn quickly; those who merely poke their heads out are still ten paces behind.

You must further turn the mechanism and shift the position, changing the constellations and displacing the stars. At such a time, the thousand eyes open at once and the myriad functions respond in unison.
Then people will know that there is [the truth] which cuts off the mysterious pass—how do you speak this single phrase? After a long silence, he said:
Iron cavalry fly amidst flashing lightning; spring winds dance upon the peach-blossom waves. Entering the hall:
On this auspicious night of the first day of the first month, the sun rises from the eastern side, illuminating Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. Turning back and circling, it points toward the center.
Sitting firmly, he cuts off the path of the Stone Bridge; ordinary beings and sages have no place to exchange positions. Buddhas and patriarchs give rise to enemies; when they meet...
Rice and hemp. When the snow melts and the spring rains pass, even the tip of the pestle produces flowers.

[The Master] ascends the hall. A monk asks, "Please, Master, speak of the mechanism that cuts off the tongue. The Master says, "Before the mountain, water flows into the village of ten thousand households."
The student said, “I do not understand. The Master said, “I am not your equal. The monk bowed, and the Master struck him. Then he said:
“When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault. A carpenter wearing a cangue reaps what he sows. If there is mind but no dharma, one receives retribution—good or foul.
If there is dharma but no mind, heaven is long and earth is enduring. When the mind arises, dharmas arise; when the crow flies, the hare runs.”
Run! When the mind ceases, phenomena cease. He performs a somersault; his mouth is like a drumstick, his brows like a broom. *Du!* Look at what kind of face and snout this is!
Have you not heard it said: "You sing the neighing of a wooden horse; I roar the bellow of a clay ox"?

Ascending the hall to see off the Supervisor of the Granary: A single grain of red rice, A few drops of ox-blood. Rely on you gentlemen to examine it closely; Even I find it difficult to distinguish or explain.
The plowman has not yet finished plowing; The sower has not ceased sowing. My eyes gaze toward the clouds in the nine heavens.
Who would disregard the heat of the three summer months? Now is precisely the time for autumn harvest. It all depends on being pure and meticulous; measure out every ounce with equal division.
Let words of "self" and "other" cease; one cannot be deceived even in a dark room. Even when drinking water, beware of choking. The superior person is satiated by the flavor of the Dharma.
The eye of the Way can illuminate all with clarity; returning, the almsbowl is full of fragrance. Sitting and severing the tongues of water and clouds, the golden-haired lion leaps at will.
Strange beasts hide in deep dens; the chestnut thorn and the diamond circle allow not even a drop of water to pass through. Cast your gaze upon the tips of the hundred grasses;
where the Seven Stars function, they cut through like the wind.
Ascending the hall: A new year has its own origins; tea is brewed and we ascend the wine tower. One pair of feet has no two legs; half a thing has three heads.

Suddenly appearing, it is difficult for the spirit to discern; meeting it, even ghosts are filled with grief. Blowing the holeless flute upside down, they beat the rhythm and dance the Liangzhou. *He!* (A shout).
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the following case: King Kaniṣka of Jibin, leaning on his sword, asked the Venerable Siṃha, "Have you attained the emptiness of the aggregates?

He replied, "I have already attained the emptiness of the aggregates. The King said, "Since you have attained the emptiness of the aggregates, have you escaped birth and death? He replied, "I have already escaped birth and death."
The King said, "Since you have already transcended birth and death, may I request your head? He replied, "Even this body is not mine; how much less so my head.
The King then struck him off, whereupon white milk surged forth several feet high and the King’s own arm fell away.

The Master said, "If I had been that mountain monk at that time, when he asked, 'Have you attained the emptiness of the aggregates? I would have simply told him: 'Put down your sword, and let us discuss it.'"

[The Master] measured [him]. Waiting for him to set the sword down, he said, "You have already attained the emptiness of the aggregates (*skandha-śūnyatā*). Having attained the emptiness of the aggregates, are you now free from birth and death?
He replied, "Bring back your sword, and I will deliberate with you. Waiting for him to withdraw the sword into its scabbard, he said, "You are already free from birth and death.
Now that you are free from birth and death, may you give me your head? He then said loudly, "This body is not mine."
"It is difficult to deal with the head, O Great Assembly. If you can deliver a 'blocking' phrase for the three turnings of the wheel, where else would there be a King of Kaśmīra coming?
Now, what do you say? After a long silence, he said: "No affairs; keep your comings and goings to a minimum."
Ascending the hall, [the Master] raised the case of Yunmen’s address to the assembly, which said: "Countless dead people lie upon the level ground;
those who can penetrate the thorn-brake forest are true adepts. At that time, a monk stepped forward and said, "If that is so, then the First Seat in the hall has something superior.
Yunmen said, "Sulu sulu. The Master remarked: "There are some who, as soon as they hear such words, immediately treat them as a profound mystery."

How wondrous and extraordinary! He often speaks further, saying that there is no unfolding of affairs, no words that meet the occasion, no realization, no speech, no affairs, no words, and no occasion—yet this is where the original source of your very lives lies.
Do you see Yunmen and this monk? It is like being before an array of a million troops, where the banners are raised and the enemy is struck down.
Leading the vanguard, the cavalry broke through the gates; blood flowed into rivers, and corpses lay strewn across the wilds.
Yet, look closely: not a single spear was moved, nor a single blade drawn; there was no shedding of blood or injury to hand. Do you all remember your dates of birth—the year, month, day, and hour?
Wait until we choose an auspicious day and time, and I shall bury you all in a single pit. It is just as Yunmen said:
"On the level ground there are countless dead; those who can penetrate the thorn-brake forest are true adepts.
Master Taiping took up this saying and said: "On the level ground, every one is a man of stature; those who can sit within the thorn-brake forest are true adepts.

Why is this so? He then spoke on their behalf: "The barrier. The Master said: "Had it not been for these subsequent words, he would have left the old barbarian [the Buddha] in doubt. One person is able to sit [therein]."

The Thorny Forest. One person penetrates the thorny forest; those who sit possess the inner and outer judgment within their skin, while those who penetrate possess the scales and armor within their bellies.
Both those who sit and those who penetrate still have something left to do. Is there one person who neither sits nor penetrates? Do you all wish to recognize this person?
[The Master] takes up his staff, places it to his left, gives a shout, and says: "Limitless winds atop the tree-tops."
[The Master] passed it by. He then made the sound of a cow’s song, saying: “Clapping the ox, go home; mouth, *ayi*. He ascended the hall.

The monk stepped forward and said, “Striking and bumping into things—all is wondrous. The Master said, “Carry it all away on a single shoulder-pole. The monk stepped forward.
