"How is it? Xī struck him with his palm. Shān said, "In ten years, will there even be anyone to serve tea?
Xī asked, "What would you do with Guǖshān? Shān laughed heartily.
The two armies clash; laughter seems like wrath. The twin brows are arched aloft, and sinews stir in the eyes. For whom are the clouds and moon over the mountain streams his companions?
North, south, east, and west—there are no neighbors near at hand.
A non-Buddhist asked the Buddha;
he did not ask whether there were words or no words. He spoke of seeing shadows and seeing whips; the pillar had its mouth hung upon the wall, and the lantern retreated three thousand paces.
The maiden emerges from samādhi;
she blocks and shatters the great void, so that even the passes and fords no longer allow passage. Mañjuśrī and Jālinīprabha travel from west back to east;
she draws her sword from between her brows and gazes repeatedly, while the maiden Gautamī stands utterly defeated in the wind.
Knock down the banner-pole at the gate;
in idle chatter you speak of the golden robe. I shall immediately knock that pole down right before you; from this point on, the natural order of kinship turns meaningless.
The cold light still presses upon people with its chill.
Hiding one’s body within the Big Dipper;

Shaoyang’s single blow is most novel and wondrous. Directly pointing it out at the gate of the bustling marketplace, he overturns the mountains and uproots the valley to fully manifest the true command.
Like a flash of lightning or a spark from flint, once gone, it is difficult to pursue.
Dongshan visited Yishan: "The eyes judge high and low; the nostrils hang horizontal. Shallow and deep, light and heavy—they do not contend much. Gnats and scorpions shoulder their way in;
the phoenix borrows the path from the roots of its teeth. He takes the long river and churns it into butter and curd; he dares take the handle of a grain of millet and..."
The stalks of grain. "The Rear Mountain is not yet a place for hiding one's body; appearing and disappearing, let it be as it may for birds and rabbits.
Sanjiao addressed the assembly, saying, "If we discuss this matter, as soon as you raise your eyebrows, you have already missed it.
Magu stepped forward and said, "I do not ask about missing it; what is this matter? Sanjiao said, "Missed it. Magu overturned [the seat].
The meditation seat—strike it at the corner!
Mists roll away and clouds disperse; thunder rolls and lightning flashes. Eyes go dark and ears go deaf; this is wrong, that is wrong—where can "wrong" or "not wrong" be placed?
Gone, staying, in great haste; silent, desolate, yet lively and agile.
Nanquan’s Beheading of the Cat:
Even if you could prop your tongue against the Brahma Heaven, I would still say my command has been carried out by half. Zhaozhou’s Wearing Straw Sandals on His Head:
This too is merely a new hole drilled through an old gourd.
The dog has no Buddha-nature.
Zhaozhou said, "The dog has no Buddha-nature. A stone ox fears not the lion’s roar; at midnight, clouds surge and waves meet the heavens.
At the sea-gate, a gale sweeps across; across the vast earth, those who study the Mysteries have no sinews in their eyes.
The world is poor. Where can one seek the mechanism of a flash of lightning? Its horns and peaks emerge from the wild grasses.
Master Ximù called to his attendant; the attendant responded. Mù said, "It is late at night and deep in silence;
let us deliberate with him."
The night is deep and quiet; let us deliberate well. Hand in hand, we shall enter the realm of intoxication. The beautiful maiden has already returned to the celestial void;
why does the foolish lad remain guarding his empty chamber?
Linji’s “True Person of No Rank”:
the True Person of No Rank is a bare lump of flesh. A lightning-fast mechanism that spins like a revolving bead-plate; the Adamantine Eye is a clay pellet.
One must look with feet sidestepping amidst a blaze of fierce flames.
Jingqing asked a monk, "What is that sound outside the gate? The monk said, "The sound of raindrops. Jingqing said, "Sentient beings are inverted;
deluded by themselves, they pursue external objects. The monk said, "I am just like this; how about you, Master? Jingqing said:
Jiubomi ji (It almost did not cause me to lose myself). The monk asked, "What is the meaning of 'It almost did not cause me to lose myself'? Qing said, "To manifest one's person may still be easy;
to express the Way in its entirety is difficult."
The sound of raindrops outside the gate: when the family is harmonious, all things are accomplished. Returning empty-handed with nothing at all—this makes one remember Jingqing.
Once, when a monk came to pay his respects to Xuansha, Xuansha said, "It is because of me that you pay your respects to me."
"Because of me, you receive my prostrations. The heavens and earth are but a grain of millet. If one wishes to eliminate the three evils, there is none better than asking Zhou Chu.
Master Xiange studied under Xuefeng for a long time; he concealed his traces in an ancient temple, where during the day he would wade for shrimp and clams to provide for his midday meal.
One night, Xianzi went to sleep on a pile of paper money offerings. Jing Huayan suspected him and entered the pile first to sit down.
When Xianzi returned at night, he pushed aside the heap of paper and asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Xianzi said:
Before the altar of the deity, he bows twice in thanks to the wine tray.

Before the deity, he pulls back the curtain and asks about the "coming from the West. Directly addressing the immediate situation, he points to the wine tray. With bare shoulders and head bowed in prostration, he pays his respects;
though calamity descends from heaven, no disaster arises.
In the room of Ciming, a basin of water was placed, with a sword laid across it. Beneath the basin were a pair of straw sandals.
Summer passes and winter comes; spring follows autumn. The evening sun goes west as the waters flow east. Where now are the warhorses of the generals?
Wild weeds and idle flowers fill the earth with sorrow.
In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the Universal Eye does not see Samantabhadra.
A solitary wild goose drifts through the cold void; step by step one pursues the empty sky to seek the traces of the goose. The straw sandals have been worn through until the heels are severed;
he sits loftily and alone upon the Great Hero Peak.
Praise for the Buddha Śākyamuni’s Appearance upon Leaving the Mountains:
How great is Śākyamuni! A sea of merit, immeasurable. In this place, vermilion is scarce; red earth is considered supreme.
I now prostrate, pay homage, and offer praise. May this remain as a model for humans and devas (Duh!).
O Great Being Avalokiteśvara!
How great is Avalokiteśvara! His merit is inconceivable. When one comes to speak of right and wrong, that which is right and wrong is precisely him.
Baguishi (Buddha-bag Monk). Respectfully following the rhyme of His Majesty, the bag is opened:
the monkey cries under the morning moon; mountains and seas hide their forms; the paths of Buddhas and demons are cut off. One after another, they are led away.
Towering and eminent—such great capacity that even a staff-blow does not turn him back; such great function that a sharp sword flows with fresh blood.
Parting from the world, he emerges from the head of Mount Kunlun, his crown capped in snow.
Master Zhigong once occupied Dulong Peak;
for three reigns he propagated the holy transformation. He tore open the old hide of the face, demanding the price of the vast heavens.
At that time, Zhang Sengyou was wrongly killed; who would have thought that now things have become even more remote? It cannot be sketched, it cannot be painted.
Three dice cast, nineteen comes up; where else can such a scene of splendor be found? A ruler, scissors, and a broom—this is the Layman Vimalakīrti.
(Requested by Zhao Guanshi for a eulogy.)
Everywhere he slandered the Sangha and reviled the Buddha; whether others held office or not, he knew it all. Subhūti was repeatedly rebuked by him, and even Gautama was hotly deceived.
Only Mañjuśrī refused to submit, venting his indignation to question him. This fellow knew he had no reason on his side, so at that time his mouth was as stiff as a millstone.
The Sage of Jinhua wards off weapons;
neither sword nor axe can strike him. Having passed through great kalpas, neither water nor fire can touch him. There is a reason for the brother-in-law and the younger uncle.
Where could one seek a Buddha’s face on a pig’s head? For two hundred years beneath Turtle Ridge, the Three Mountains have relied [upon him].
The old waters flow eastward.

If the Patriarch Bodhidharma had not been scrutinized by the Emperor of Liang, would he have consented to come to Shaoshi Mountain to sit in the cold? It caused the Second Patriarch to lose his mind, as he was... [by another].
To call him "Dharma" is for the old and decrepit Saltan Abbot to act out of ignorance;
he broke his fan searching for a rhinoceros calf—yet even so, there remains a lingering influence and a residual majesty. *Phat!*
*Dārimani*. Master Xuefeng visited Daowu of Touzi three times and went personally to Dongshan nine times. As for the "first phrase that is not the last," let it be as it is.
Covering earth and covering heaven—three wooden balls open the eyes of ghosts; without cause, they are bound and cast down into the human world.

The long-bearded monk possesses a towering divine radiance reaching ten thousand fathoms; his beard and whiskers are matted together like a woven rug. He cries out his grievance before Mount Ruiying, able to say:
A fragment of snow upon a red brazier. I now bow my head to inquire after your tracks; I dare to drive an iron stake into empty space.

Before Linji’s "blow of the razor" was even raised, fresh blood was already dripping; as soon as the "poisoned drum" was struck, corpses lay strewn across the entire world. His faculty was like splitting bamboo.
His mouth is like a drumstick. Two hundred years ago, he was killing people and setting fires in Jiangxi and Hunan;

three thousand *li* away, in Shandong and Hebei, he seized drums and snatched banners. He overturned the great ocean and sat atop Mount Sumeru. At the head of the green meadows, he wields the true command;

in his white-thief’s hand, he seeks advantage. Pshaw! You little fellow—let me ask you this: *(Note: The term "白拈" [báiniān] refers to a "white-thief," one who steals by stealth rather than force. The phrase "青草步頭" [qīngcǎo bùtóu] likely alludes to a specific place or a symbolic site of authority.)*
Blind! To whom was the Eye of the True Dharma entrusted?
Master Yunmen wore Muzhou’s tattered straw sandals backward; he rolled Xuefeng’s rotten ball across. When the poison-bird flies through the sky, the grass does not grow.
When the venomous dragon enters the water, all the fish die; Śāṇavāsa alone picks up the challenge to test the barrier of men. Moving both with and against the current, he cuts off coming and going.
His legacy still leaves behind a chilling wind; even to this day, there remains a trace of his brilliance.

Master Puhua was afflicted with a feverish madness; he kicked over the rice table, his feet slipped and stumbled, and he performed somersaults, ruining the lifelong Chan practice of Linji and silencing the samādhi-mouth of Panshan.
At times he appeared good, yet not necessarily good; at times he appeared evil... [and so on].
He must have been a scoundrel. At one time he was carrying a broken wooden clapper, chasing after village feasts at Dabeisi Temple; even until now, he has had no clue.
Master Mokpyeong’s peaks towered high and his depths were profound; his countenance was ancient and his spirit pure. When thirsty, he had only rice-water; for a meal, there were no choice delicacies.

At the head of the dragon-couch, he flaunted his straw sandals; before the imperial boat, he emerged with half his cloud-like robe visible. Raising the oars, one lost the source; the bolt was fastened.
The rope has already been exposed; shifting the boat to different waters, his eyes turn upward and his sinews stiffen. How could one dare say this does not require the labor of the axe?
This is what is called Muping (Wood-Flat), the Boatman Monk.
The veteran of old relied on Jia Shan; his entire mechanism was exhausted, and a deep grievance was formed. Father south, son north—where is the home?
He shifts the celestial pivot and turns the terrestrial axis upside down.
The wind sweeps through the cloudless sky as the small boat tilts; in the depths of misty waves, he makes his living.
With hands that have severed the double-barreled mechanism of the spinning line, he plucks out the sand from within the eyes of the black dragon.
For eighteen years, Master Xianglin Yuan practiced what kind of Chan? The profound essence of Yunmen is meant for others to transmit. Suddenly, he struck the great stone tune;
brand new, like a mountain ablaze in the month of December.
Master Yangqi’s dispatch:
Yangqi’s one-legged fortress terrifies the little fellow Linji. The thorny briar and the golden ring are the price of the goods;
with the land vast and people sparse, to whom shall they be sold? Taking only these broken straw sandals and clay pellets, he exchanges them at the crossroads.
Three hundred loads of eyeballs were obtained; neither man perceived them nor did the ghosts know of it. Alas! Returning at midnight, the sun is already at noon;
the void remains as it was, yet painted with蛾眉 (fashioned eyebrows).
Master Yùquán Hào applies the teaching in reverse and employs it contrarily; he alone draws forth and upholds it alone. Crows fly and hares run; tigers gallop and dragons race.

As the movement of the celestial dial shifts, the winter solstice arrives. His coarse cloth trousers remain unwashed, with nothing to replace them. Let him teach as he will, scattering earth and tossing sand.
The self-mastery bowl rings; the *piśāca* boils. I now prostrate to the Tathāgata Lokeśvararāja.
*Gate gate pāragate*.
Preceptor Dianne (invited by Tu-du Yan-zhu to compose this eulogy).
The source of the Washed Brocade River has surging, furious waves that swallow the Three Gorges; the abyss of Hezhou Bay has giant billows leaping into the sky, connecting to the Five Lakes.
Seizing the two markers, he casts them away with ease at his hand. Examining the scarlet clouds, he further finds the worthy one without a skull—his head is square and his robes are intact.

Squatting upon the mat of the "dead mind," he faces it and drinks the poison of the *viṣa* to his fill. With hawk-like brows and an elephantine countenance, he enters the tiger’s den of Zhantang to sever its life-force and lose his own body.
He penetrates the core of Huanglong’s Three Barriers and sheds the mold of Linji’s ten generations. Ox-heads and horse-heads appear and disappear;
the sickness of the Buddhas and the sickness of the Patriarchs are cured. I bow my head to the blind donkey; there is no water for the accidental extermination of his clan.
Scales and shells; the crags are smeared with lethal poison. When principle is severed and emotion forgotten, one directly receives the entrustment.

Master Dahui’s practice of Chan lacked essential principles; he studied the Buddha-dharma without merit, undermining the Way of Yangqi and extinguishing the Linji lineage. He simply held up [the mind] directly.
The Buddhas and Patriarchs do not violate their commands; they act with wild abandon and madness while dwelling on the peaks of Shuangjing.
In the midst of casual ease, they snatch away the monk’s cord of fixed destiny, taking error for truth. His fame reaches the Nine Palaces—A-he-he! Do you see?
With the bamboo staff, whether one strikes or retreats, one loses the money and incurs the penalty. The Way of Heaven allows no return; the dragon pearl is free from flaw or blemish.
The Verse on the Śūraṅgama Sūtra: The Six Sense Organs—
The Eye Cannot See.
Aniruddha, with his divine eye, perceives that the great trichiliocosm is contained within the tip of a single hair; he might as well speak of an *āmala* fruit in the palm of his hand.
Countless sentient beings are thus deceived by this heat.
One without ears can hear;

the Dragon Bānaṃda can listen. When Vimalakīrti’s tongue is tied, how can he debate? Reaching the place where the waters end and the mountains exhaust themselves, empty space remains as it was, filling heaven and earth.
The Gaṅgā Goddess, who lacks a nose, does not smell fragrances; she is like a poor man who has suddenly become wealthy.
Having once been rebuked on the banks of the lotus river, misfortune arising from her own household turned into auspiciousness.

The one with a distinct tongue who knows flavors is Kāvaṇyapati; he knows these flavors—bitter, astringent, salty, and sour—yet how could they be there? With a single lift, he can reach the Brahma Heaven;
he transcends and realizes the Tathāgata’s true meaning.
The *śūnyatā* who perceives touch is not the body;
the *śūnyatā* who perceives touch is not the body. Bar the gates, block the doors, and plant thorny brambles. To capture empty space at such a distance is like encountering him;
yet even such an encounter is but a casual acquaintance.
The mental faculty (*manas*) cognizes the golden-headed snake, and as the mental faculty ceases, it clearly and perfectly cognizes the snowless place; the sole of the straw sandal snaps,
the eyelids droop, and the staff of Sudhana grows three joints.
Zihu has a dog: it takes people’s heads at the top, hearts in the middle, and feet at the bottom.
Zihu has a dog that takes people’s heads; with a great laugh and a long song, he emerges from the painted pavilion.
As the setting sun and severed clouds join the mountain peaks, the cowherd returns home riding his ox backward.
Zihu has a dog that takes people’s hearts. It is said that the Yellow River is bottomless and deep.
After the words were left upon the top of the *huabiao* pillar, there has been no further news until the present day.
Zihu has a dog that seizes people’s feet; after the dance ends, it allows you three or two more tunes. Though you try to pull back from its jade stirrups and golden saddle, it will not turn;
last night, as always, it slept among the reeds.

Hattō’s three phrases include one that does not enter the ears of a donkey. Before the sun reaches its zenith or the moon begins to wane, there is no room for display. Once you have stepped out the gate, you will realize the scales are tipped;
yet before even stepping out, I shall present them to you.
I have the phrase that cuts off the water and halts the wheel; the paths of humans and devas are severed, and faith comes but rarely.
Carelessly leaning upon the staff that overhangs the head, the deep sands within the gate are covered with rheumy eyes.
I have a verse for fishing for the moon amidst the mist: mountains crumble and seas run dry—this is my lifelong vocation. In the end, both the poor and the wealthy know little of gratitude;
gathering it all back, we are but one family.
One phrase from Xiatang divides into three: forged of pure steel, cast from raw iron. At midnight, a tortoise sheds its shell and flies away;
stars are scattered like clouds, leaving no place to be found.
Practicing the four modes of deportment (1,735 words), returning at noon to strike the eighth watch. Amidst the wild weeds, he binds his tongue and speaks of non-arising.
Abiding. A harmonious voice blocks the path from whence one comes. The handle of the Dipper hangs low; wind and clouds always fill his belly. Seated.
The coming and going of ordinary beings and sages is like turning a millstone. Desist! Desist! He invites others, yet none are willing to pass through.
Lying down, who knows that diligence has become indolence? Mindfulness of Mahā. It is better to return and endure hunger.
Not manifesting fame: Verses on the Invitation by the Great Patron (five stanzas).
The great capacity responds perfectly, transcending names and forms; the scenery fills the capital to the horizon. Last night, at the wine tower, the spring was deep.
At dawn, one sees Great Vairocana directly before oneself;

within the workings of both adverse and favorable conditions, all is Chan. Remaining at home does not hinder the conditions for leaving it behind. Master and son, the Pang family, sit together in a circle;
suddenly awakening, the discourse on non-arising is complete.
If you wish to practice the direct pointing of the *Sūtra of Holding One*, the sacred texts upon palm leaves fill precious caskets.
Without self, without person, and without a life-principle—dust mote by dust mote, world-system by world-system, all is Gautama.
If one can transform objects, one is immediately a Tathāgata; the True Eye opens upon a heap of refuse.
Following the inverted views of sentient beings, may the numinous terrace be manifested everywhere.

Retribution varies and circumstances differ; what use is this weary life within its cage? If you wish to know the true Buddha of your own nature, it is entirely contained within a single thought at dawn or dusk.
Answer: For the Layman Songchuang, ten thousand functions are extinguished and the eye’s field is empty; when not a single point arises, with whom can one share?
Before even asking Vimalakīrti, he has already sealed his mouth—how could such a one be called a mountain-dwelling elder?
The single word from Master Chaoran at Hushui was personally received; from Tongcheng, a thousand li away, we hear again. Your rhymes and phrasing are fresh and incisive;
I wonder with whom you have been debating, Master?
Answer: The Minister Zeng Hui is a diamond eye that encompasses heaven and earth; he reforges and re-refines the iron caltrops until his entire being is cast away without a trace.
From this moment on, the blind donkey loses its total capacity. This is the lively, liberated path beyond the ordinary—its gathering and releasing must be vast indeed.
Taking a step, stamping mud and stamping water—observe this before your very eyes. The faces of the sun and moon vanish in mutual reversal;

freed from the cage and loosened from the bridle, all names and models are severed. When the staff and the shout race one another, is there anything attained? Not falling into the gate of transformation, what matter is accomplished?
Within the purple silk curtain, true pearls are scattered.
Entrusting this to Grand Marshal Wang Quanji:

How can one repay [his kindness]? When the law is fully applied, there are no subjects left; yet he refuses to rest. Unable to remain within the Golden Horse Gate or the Jade Hall, he continues as before to peddle Yangzhou from within his own house.
In response to Ge, the Circuit Intendant:
The *Hilara* "True Eye" manifests within the dust; the mysterious mechanism of the successive patriarchs is raised beyond the norm. Look at it while the drum beats—the grievance remains unavenged;
from the beginning, red earth has been used to paint the winnowing basket.
To Li Caiweng, Instructor of the Imperial Academy:
I have studied the Buddha’s teachings for several autumns; In dreams I write upon the void, yet upon waking, I let it rest.
If you wish to understand the verse on the extinction of the Three Wu clans, You must personally arrive at the Hundred Flowers Isle.

An Inscription Requested by Zhu Boke (with Preface) The Layman Wujū (Cornerless), who adjudicates affairs, possesses a Daoist resonance that transcends his peers and a natural endowment that stands out from the crowd. His loyalty and righteousness pierce through the sun and moon.

Filial piety and fraternal respect penetrate both the human and divine realms. Having found the proper method for instructing his sons and the correct principles for governing his household, he established Yingzhao Monastery at the foot of Fenghuang Mountain beside the tomb of his late father, to perpetually welcome monastics and thereby provide spiritual support for the ancestral way. Huiyuan requested that the honors accorded to his ancestors be discontinued, and this was granted.
The gist is this: I have retired here of my own accord; not long after settling in, I was summoned by imperial decree to Cold Spring.
Upon my departure, he requested words, so I wrote down these verses as they came to me.

Seeking seclusion beneath Mount Fenghuang, he turns his body once more within the city of Magadha. Where is it as stars and lightning flash across one another? How can one describe this inverted application of the pivot?
For the layman, the gate is high and there is no divergent teaching; where the mountain monk travels, he is liberated from root and dust.
With the wind as companion and the moon as neighbor, the three-eyed Mahesvara smiles as if in anger. In years to come, he shall again take up his staff...
Tilting the canopies, we meet; clapping our hands and raising our brows, a smile breaks anew.
County Magistrate Qian prays for progeny and seeks a panegyric:
"A bright pearl remains in the palm, yet it might still be dropped; A radiant jade is within the pouch, never losing its timing. Fortunately, there is the Jade Ring of Guanyin."
[The Master] said, "Hand! Why trouble yourself further by reciting the poem about 'the dream of a cub'?
Wang, the Magistrate, requested a verse. (By the Layman Wuyi):
"I bestow not a single dharma upon others; how could there be two kinds of speech? The Layman’s gate is high; whenever he meets someone, he speaks thus."
The stone beam is broken; the eyelids are crossed. The lion roams alone without a companion.
When Magistrate Ge Tongpan requested instruction on the karmic conditions of "neither mind nor Buddha," the Master showed it to him with a verse:
"Mind is Buddha, eyebrows trailing the ground; Neither Buddha nor mind, both eyes crossed. In the dream of a butterfly, ten thousand homes."
The village. The night is at its third watch under the branch of the cuckoo tree.
Director Li’s "Cattle Herding" painting is said to depict the water-buffalo of Mt. Mui. He loses to the black dot, yet he wins the tally. It is not the water-buffalo of Mt. Mui.
The ox. He wins from others, yet he loses his white tally. Black and white are not yet distinguished, but the horns are already revealed.
Win or lose is not what covers the head; the ox-cord has been severed and the nose-ring is gone. With tail swishing and head held high, he attains freedom.

Amidst the boundless green grass of the clouded mountains, the fragrant waters flow gently with the mist. Let him loose when hungry; gather him in when full. Raising a great bellow as he charges forth in the wind.
The sound of the flute; turning my head toward the mountain of my home, all affairs have ceased.

In response to Mr. Shi’s “White Lotus,” the Jade Maiden tilts her crown, shining bright upon the night pond. Snow spreads across the immortal’s palm, offending the fragrance of autumn. In the fifth month of Jiangnan, the winds are many.
Elegant and naturally radiant, she required no makeup to beautify her.
At first, she drifted from the Lotus Society across the pond; now she has been drawn into the fragrant breath of the assembly of sages.
The powder and dew have already vanished with the clouds and rain, yet her crystalline form remains as a trace of her slight adornment.

At Guoqing Temple, the bridge of the monk’s staff spans five peaks where the emerald hues are crushed like indigo. The sound of the two mountain streams vibrates like the ringing of a staff; within them dwells an old *bimbara* who plays a holeless flute upside down.
He does not permit the drifting clouds to accompany him on his return—whom will come now to tread upon the traces of the verdant moss?
At the Twin Trees, the Unattached Pavilion stands loftily apart;
all manner of beings flock there. The myriad phenomena are submerged in a state of serene joy; the lake and sky float far upon the water. The rocks on the shore are soaked by deep clouds;
as the rain clears, the moonlight penetrates through. The wind stirs the shadows of the mountains; the spirit soars beyond the eight directions. Vast and penetrating is the wondrously luminous mind.
Wandering through the Caves of Liu and Ruan, clouds deepen and dew grows cold; no one dares to enter. Along the narrow path, dark clouds and emerald mist seem to obscure the way.
Having paid my respects to the traces of immortals from ancient times, I listen to the cries of monkeys amidst the shadows of the jagged peaks.

At Nanxiang Temple, countless green mountains accompany my journey; I shall further wash my dusty cap in their clear, shallow waters. To bathe in the flowing stream and rinse my teeth upon the rocks is truly my own affair;
I shall purchase a plot of idle land to cultivate right here.

Mirror Hermitage’s ancient mirror has been shattered since its arrival at Xu Da’s hermitage; though not a single autumn hair remains, his vision is still vast. He no longer remembers the dreams of three lifetimes across rivers and lakes;
of wind and moon, there remains but a single fishing rod.
Universal blessings are shared;
beneath the sea-tower red dust rises, while atop the mountain white waves fly. If one can understand it thus, one will fall into hell for eternal kalpas.
Inscribed on an Ink Bamboo Painting.

The brush-tip is imbued with divine spirit; it excels in the wondrous efficacy of cosmic transformation. It plays like a azure dragon trailing its tail, and turns its back upon the bright moon as it sways in the wind.
Sparse shadows stir soundlessly amidst the cold ink; slender branches, bearing leaves, seem to overturn the autumnal sky.

The fragrant breeze from the Xiangfeng Hall of Fushō-ji wafts through the celestial capital; it drifts lightly, filling one’s sleeves. It rises loftily before the time of Vimalacitra and transcends levelly the era of Prabhūtaratna.
Not falling into the four seasons, it is willing to vie with the hundred flowers. How could the sense of smell ever contain it? How could one reproach the River God?
In a state of serene intoxication, the water-mirror is empty; the clouds grow cold as the fragrant breeze permeates.
As Miaoxi returned south, [the author] welcomed him with these verses:

Having heard that the Celestial Edict has descended upon the inner palace, I know for certain that the traces of the clouds will now meet at the pivot of power. There is no need to inquire further about the thousand-year-old Bronze Horses;
A single segment of this radiant splendor has fundamentally returned to its source.
Next, following the rhyme of Master Wanian Ben, I have composed this verse:
"To have attained the head is precisely when one should investigate. Relying on another's gate, one is not yet conversant with it. The Master thus has his 'sleeping upon the clouds' verse;
he must surely laugh at Śāriputra’s talk within a dream."
A single hill and a single gully open with laughter and talk; what need is there to meet and grasp the wine cup? Before and after the rain, the fangs and claws remain;
they polish the spring colors finely, awaiting your arrival.

Entrusted to Master Miaochan of Zhongzhu, the lake and mountains have gained an old Demon King. His tongue rolls like wind and thunder, his eyes emit light. Turning his back on the Dharma Hall, he undergoes another thorough examination;
one knows not who will share the spoils with him.
Entrusting this to Master Quan of Daochang:
with a snowy summit like Mount Kunlun, he gazes intently; the ten-headed rākṣasa smiles with an open countenance. You shall enter first where the cauldron of boiling water is cold;
when the eyes are crossed, wait for me to come.
To Venerable Ren of Andang: A single blow that strikes the mark—none of the thousand sages can peer into it.
Wearing the seal of no-pattern, donning rag robes, he sits enthroned upon the palace of the Māra King.
They open the door of false views; they speak of dhyāna and the Way. With foul mouths and stinking teeth, they debate the mind and discuss nature.

They scatter excrement and urine; they pull plows and climb trees. They bend and break the scale-beam; they defy and oppose the Buddhas and Patriarchs. Their actions are perverse and contrary; they are no longer fit for the Hall of Benevolence.
Who could it possibly be? When the music ends and the wine is drained, no one understands; with a broken heart, she still paints her蛾眉 (yúméi) brows. Sent to the Head Seat:
On the peak of White Stone Mountain, there are many monks. The clay ox has sucked dry the waves in the well. In years to come, the cloth bag shall be opened again.
Mouth. The Buddhas and Patriarchs, as before, could do nothing about it.

Sending off the Head Seat Neng to reside at Zituo, he drove the plow and seized the food, continuing the heart-lamp. As they exchanged and raced one another, the goods increased; the Way is great and cannot be known—vainly one hopes for it.
In the north, his merit expanded as he respectfully bowed to those of high standing in Lingnan.

He saw Elder Xuan depart for Linquan, where he shed his cage and snapped his reins, changing his skin and fur; though the waters are distant and the mountains long, the Way remains naturally lofty. This is the simple and unadorned family style, maintained according to one’s lot.
Unfurling [the sail]: for a moment, the great butcher’s blade is bent to slaughter a chicken.
Sending off Elder Jiufeng to his old retreat:
the Iron-Faced Persian rides the raging surges; as the black wind rises, the waves grow high. He steers his small skiff backward and draws forth his golden [spear].
The arrowhead: It is just like a general entering a desolate wasteland.

When sent forth, the great function is manifest before one; the entire body is it. When the sentiments of sage and ordinary are exhausted, shadows cannot remain. At the very bottom of the almsbowl, there are three thousand [worlds].
The Dhātu: At the tip of the staff lie the four hundred prefectures; the clouds are companions, the moon is a peer. Upon reaching home, there is yet another road that pierces the heavens;
holding fast the secure barrier, one rolls the embroidered ball.
Sent to the Eminent Layman Yang:
It has been ten years since we parted; in poverty, I have not had a single night’s restful sleep. Please come to join me in a night conversation, and let us together sip from the clear spring.
Sent to Master Yuan.
In studying the Buddha, take awakening as the standard. Empty words do not enter the public gate. Behold Wang Xizhi’s "Divine Calligraphy"—a single dot penetrates the stone by three fen.
This is sent to the Venerable Administrator Wanhua, with a brief note for Layman Miaojing.
The path across the stone bridge was perilous as he entered with his body horizontal; the peak of Ox Star was high as he gazed upward with his face turned back.
Were it not for the worthy Prefect Lü Qiū, who else could have idly recognized the aged Fēnggān?
Seeing off the two Zen practitioners, Kakua and Kinkei, from the land of Japan on their journey to Tiantai:
these disciples of the Buddha have come directly from Japan; as gods and men follow their steps, they exclaim in wonder: "A single stroke brings forth the dancing Golden Ox;
before the eyes of a thousand sages, the true eye is opened."
Killing people and setting fires—this is great compassion. Neither Chan nor Teachings can match this Way.
With a single roar from level ground, Śākyamuni and Maitreya raise their banners of surrender.
The Buddha’s disciple has flown his sails across the sea to arrive; well would he carry his flask and staff up to Mount Tiantai. The National Teacher still leaves behind his numinous traces;
the precious stupa stands majestic, its face turned fully open.

The school outside the teachings brought by Bodhidharma from the West leaves no room for words or explanations; therein he established his full merit. A single transmission, pointing directly, is the eye of the entire body—who can believe that it has been thoroughly exhausted to the very marrow since of old?
Next, Master Chen’s verse on the same rhyme:
"Baofu asked idly of the past: 'Ehu suddenly entered the Sangha Hall. There is no profound meaning upon the center of the scale;
Do not mistake it for a trace of fragrance on the hook.'"

Holding up a single phrase, one is liberated from the biased and the orthodox; the wind, moon, and the hundred rivers naturally bring serene joy. Uruvilvā Kāśyapa did not dare to open his mouth lightly;
with palms joined and fists raised, he stood before the Buddha.

Turning the mechanism and reversing its use follows from former matters; seizing the food and driving the plow tests the true master. As stars and lightning flash across, the profound path is cut off;
let them glare with bared teeth at the deep sands.
Next, the Chan Master Chen Pan’s verse on the same rhyme:

"Slandering the Buddha-dharma of others and destroying the Chan of others— The sword-trees and knife-mountains stand right before one's eyes. A tortoise at the bottom of a well swallows the night moon;
A wooden man turns his head and wails to the azure heavens."
Showing the non-abiding man of the Way, he shatters the pristine Chan of the past. Ten thousand functions converge before the skull; his body lies across, blocking the path from whence one came.
A single phrase meets the occasion: the sun shines brightly in the sky.
Showing the water-mill and the pestle:
when the wheel turns, it is difficult to draw near; standing still at the place of rest, there is no room for taking charge. Grinding flour and pounding rice are matters of long-standing practice;
smashing through the whole lump does not hinder anything at all.
Visiting Hongfu Temple to Address the Assembly:

I have already grown old in my ten years of dwelling in the mountains; Half my life spent as a wandering monk, yet I have not forgotten the essential function [of Zen]. This morning, once again, I dreamt of Mount Fushan;
In secret, I write of this sorrowful heart—to whom shall I send it?
Seeing Off Master Yang on His Return to Shu:

The dragon gallops and the tiger strides—where does the Way remain? Are you willing to turn the divine elixir to serve the Most Honored One? When the command descends upon the mountain home, it is fulfilled in a single word;
The sun and moon within the ladle are divided within the palm. In years past, we clasped hands as we ascended the golden hall; Today, we raise our fists.
Leaving the Forbidden Gate, I wish to see you off as you seek your old hermitage; the flowing waters of Peach Blossom Spring lead to the village of apricot blossoms.
To the Chan practitioner Ji, I send these words:
by the side of the Gusu Terrace we shall meet again in ill fortune, and before Mount Haiyong our circumstances shall be the same. Returning from a dream of my native land, spring has already arrived.
He departs; water and clouds gaze upon one another as a single sail catches the wind.

Sending off the Chan guest Huichong—Old Chong’s inquiry into the Dharma is like a spring thunderclap. Wrathful Nanda and Upananda cannot pull him back; dragon-sprints and tiger-strides rush forth like split arrows.
Urged on! Violent winds and raging rains topple the mountains and peaks. I too, according to my capacity, respond with the perfect pivot: when emerging, I must seize; when battling, I must conquer.
Like a pearl rolling upon a tray, or a tray rolling over a pearl—stars fly and lightning whirls, leaving nothing behind.

In years to come, while others scold the wind and revile the rain, I shall sit loftily and alone atop the Wondrous Peak, waiting to watch them kill and set fires, as my two piercing eyes blaze like fire.
The Great Void.

Having sent off the Chan practitioner who has not yet clarified the fixed contemplation of the three thousandfold world-system, look now at the eighteen rapids of Jiangxi, which reflect the city beneath Mount Fuyong.
The moon; within the reflection of golden ripples, the cold of the wheat-ripening season.

To the Zen practitioner who comes with an iron-and-stone mind to inquire of the Way: how shall I repay one so skilled at tuning the golden arrowhead? Under the staff and the shout, follow the current.
Entering, he leans back and topples over the Water-Ox of Mount Gui.

This single phrase is fully raised, transcending all comparison; when the myriad functions fail to reach it, one begins to pass through the ford. The man of the Way possesses another, extraordinary "heavenly eye";
with no fixed home throughout the four seas, all are his kin.
Looking into the mirror, withdraw it entirely and investigate thoroughly. The three blows at Xinfeng were truly difficult to swallow. In the end, there is no room for either enmity or gratitude;
one merely wins descendants who grow increasingly foolish.

The six sense objects are not evil, yet the triggering mechanism is difficult to fathom; the samādhi is soundless, its subtlety beyond exhaustion. Having cast off the entire body at once, all traces of its mark are forgotten;
where can one find the tracks of the blind donkey?
Hanging on a precipice, he grasps the rhythm and dances the *Santai*; the dead tiger, startled and frantic, has its eyes opened wide.
In a sacred ground, no ordinary weeds grow; indeed, he has personally seen Xiatang come.
The *akṣa* fruit protrudes before the wind; beyond the norm, the "thorn-bush" Zen is directly raised. At the tip of every blade of grass, the mysterious path is cut off;
having arrived home, it is not worth half a cent.

Manifesting as a beast, shrouded in fur and bearing horns, one studies non-arising; traversing the sword-trees and knife-mountains in succession, one does not swallow the thorny jujube at the Five Peaks—
how could one know that at midday, the third watch is struck?
The body is like a coconut; the gallbladder is like heaven. He shouts, "Come and study the thorn-bush Chan! Press down the clouds and lightly pass through;
the mouth-skin has always been right at the lips.
Linji’s family would often travel with their alms bowls; when one who knew the Way saw them, they did not treat him lightly.
Closing the gate, they returned home to prepare a fine feast—a bounty that remains satiating even unto this day.
The staff supports the root, yet it cannot be lifted; the bottomless bowl returns full. Why does Vimalakīrti feel such empty desolation?
After the weeping ceases, even Xiangyan knows nothing more. The hair is disheveled and the countenance is discernible; the ears are prominent and cannot be scrutinized.
The ferryman’s boat returns; people ask the way. To the south of Hanshan, west of the stone bridge.
A glance arises before the pivot of the mechanism; The mirror is drawn from behind that glance. The Dharma-body hides within the Big Dipper; The boatman sails down to Yangzhou.
The four seas have the wind as their line; the three mountains have the moon as their hook. Turning the spearhead to strike the dragon’s tail, one waits but a moment to catch the giant turtle.

When the young scholar Hong requested a verse, among the assembly of sages he alone was granted permission. Upon the Empty King’s command, he swiftly turned his body; he must surely possess a different way of grasping the clouds.
The Hand. This points to the person beyond the limit of awe-inspiring sound (Vaiśravaṇa).
Master Chen the Daoist requested a verse;

the Master’s wondrous Way was transmitted all at once. I too, according to the occasion, struck upon both ends. Having cast aside the "Wordless" of the Minister of Agriculture, [the hand] is revealed.
Seal. From this point, the waves of the hundred rivers cease.

The monk Dongyuan Guanghua requests a verse on the ancient hall, its charred remains uncounted years old. Cold light reflects one another, chilling the Ox and Cow constellations. When the opportunity arises, there will be one who wields the axe.
The hand. Azure tiles and vermilion eaves pierce the azure sky.
To the one who delivers this discourse:

the scholar of West Lake possesses a wondrous celestial mechanism; his tongue rolls like wind and thunder, and his lips fly with eloquence. As for seizing the steed, it has not yet been heard of at the desert frontier.
Cold. Breaking through the pass first, the battle clouds hang low. The sages of past and present may be counted by you; that the waters are distant and the mountains long, I alone know.
There is no need to seek old hermitages with white hair; in the end, who is right and who is wrong?
Four Poems on the Fisherman by Master Deshan: "Shoo!
You fisherman from Zhachuan, you are quite a rascal. Carrying a load of door-knocking tiles upon your staff, Before even being served a meal, you already open your mouth."
Hush! Put it all down. From now on, the price of "granny's cake" will rise; it is unbearable that Longtan came in person.
True gold and gravel are both cast aside; from the Buddhas' and Patriarchs' staffs, rain pours down—there is nothing to grasp. Originally, it was never a matter of "zhi-hu-zhe."
The sixty blows of the mountain cane from Master Linji are a truly heavy reward; with eyes as clear as a rush-sandals, he distinguishes dragons from elephants.

He went straight to Dayu to display his skill, yet his timing was not swift enough; though separated by a single mat, he still knew how to scratch an itch. How could one dare look up at the heights of Huangbo Mountain? It is personal.
If they were not father and son, who would come and go? Habitually grasping the tiger’s whiskers, one forgets thought and conception. A slap across the cheek;
with a single clap of thunder atop a thousand peaks. — Chan Master Fuguo.
Setting out toward the south, he clarifies his own self; at the peak of the White Lotus Mountain, he meets one with pierced ears. Blinking an eye and raising an eyebrow—neither is it so.
Knowing shame is rare; how lamentable that Shaoshi split the skin and marrow! The fame of Xiaoyu has not yet ceased; why does Shannan delude himself regarding the profound intent?
A single phrase, freshly forged, finally reaches the bottom. Within the Zen grove, clouds are overturned and rain falls.
The wind and waves arise.
Xiatang describes himself:
"I do not lie down in the depths of the reeds; I move my boat as far as the heart of the waves. I have caught a scaled fish of such magnitude."
Great! There is no place for trade. Pushing open the screen, we face the moon and divide it equally. We dance our oars and sing long songs, their sound spreading far and wide.

Heart-intoxicated by the rivers and mountains, we sit with eyes fixed upon them. Fortunately, sons and grandsons are all here together at the flower-adorned rudders. In harmony they respond; the prow is turned, and we return home.
A Zen practitioner wrote this eulogy for his own portrait, requesting praise:
"In his youth he relied upon Yuanwu; in his later years he dwelt among groves and springs. He left no door unopened to resolve his grievances; his cry of innocence resounds throughout the world."
The Celestial Son’s eye, Mahesvara, gazes upon the golden ring and the thorny *karkarava* of Dhyana. This secret manual of the immortals is not transmitted even between father and son.
On level ground he unfurls the hand that binds the tiger; in an ordinary moment, he thrusts forth the fist that blocks the chest.
Walking alone through the forest of false views, he sits high upon the palace of the Demon King. He preaches a Chan that deceives the common folk and deludes the sages;

he manifests the faces of yakṣas and rākṣasas. He overturns the great mountains and acts with reckless folly to the very bottom; he shatters the sturdy barrier and emerges suddenly, beyond discernment.
A-he-he! Do you see? When one reaches the river, the land of Wu ends; across the shore, the mountains of Yue abound.
To call it a painting is an error; to praise it is an error. Not recognizing the clam-shell sieve, one calls it Puhua’s wooden clapper.
Now, for the time being, its head is not the head and its feet are not the feet. Fearing that people might lack faith, I establish this as a covenant.

Clearing the thorny forest, blocking the paths of humans and devas; seizing the essential thread of the tradition, they stride with broad steps. The wind is high, the clouds are still, and the crescent moon hangs low;
they walk straight toward the golden wheel at the edge of the waters. Upon arriving home, there is no ground left over; when the sun rises, affairs arise once more.
He cuts off the seed of the Buddha and destroys the family estate; it is none other than Yangqi, the fifth generation. Zen practice is but wind passing by one’s ear;
the Buddha-dharma is a film over the eye. When asked what he has to offer others, he still possesses his own personal red seal.
The great earth is a single whole body; empty space cuts off the four quarters. Not recognizing the "pine tree," one calls it "three catties of hemp.
At times of excellence, there is tenfold elegance; at times of adversity, there is a single flavor of coarseness.

Carelessly pulling a plow up into the Buddha hall, riding a horse within a bowl out of inspiration, urinating and defecating on level ground—one knows whether another is real or false. O Zen practitioner!
To depict it thus is like a torch atop a tiger’s head.
Why did you shave your hair so early? Why did you hear the Way so late? A fierce tiger leaving the forest relies on the mountain; a venomous snake blocking the road opens its eyes.

Whether heavy or light, there is no leakage; whether intended or unintended, it immediately takes hold. When one asks about Lü Wang’s *Six Tactics*, how does it compare to Huang Gong’s *Three Strategies*?
To grasp firmly or to let go entirely depends on you; as for blending the mud and mixing the water, who else could do it? The entire great earth is gathered into these three matters.
Nan! Two eyebrows burst forth from the void; there is no avoiding them—seize upon them with fierce mindfulness! Startled back from the spring dream, one returns riding a black ox on its back.

Grasping the Wheel-Turning King’s sword, the mechanism of life and death is fully manifest; casting open the true eye, who is it that stands before you? From the beginning, there has been nothing to avoid.
A taboo name. This matter is beyond deliberation. To whom can Zhaozhou’s hidden intent be told?

Even one with an iron heart would break with grief. Coldly laughing at Deshan, he hotly deceives Linji; head heavy and tail light, the bowl rings and the gruel boils. Attendant Ming penetrates the celestial mechanism;
an eighty-year-old old man skillfully paints his eyebrows. He overturns the lion’s den and rides backward upon a blind donkey.

The wind is high and the clouds are thin; the dew makes the mist clear. Sitting upon the stone beneath the pines, I listen to the sounds above the pines. Hearing, knowing, seeing, and perceiving have no interference;
as summer passes and winter comes, there is nowhere for the snow to fall. Eight-armed Nātha looks on with a twisted face;
the seven-starred sharp sword cuts through with a sound.
Painting [this] is unbearable; it discards wisdom and mingles with poison. To praise it is not right. Loathing the shackles of the body, one sits at the site of enlightenment through thirteen stages.
How could the morning and evening meals ever suffice? Daytime is spent traveling by night, and one takes shelter in darkness until dawn.
Passing through the thorn forest, the eyes of Xie Luo are blinded; picking up the broken sand bowl, he sets down the leaking oil lamp.
Only Secretary Zhou alone recognizes him with his full capacity. It is truly laughable that the Great Being Yun Huang once went barefoot to pay homage to Mañjuśrī.
Leaning against Yunmen’s “withdrawal and inspection,” he pushes aside Linji’s “host and guest” Chan. A single spark of lion’s blood transforms into donkey’s milk;
a tiny drop of phoenix glue mends the broken strings. Attendant Chun sheds all karmic conditions; the Persian picks up the bag of invitations.
The Qilin laughs beneath the moon, its voice piercing the heavens.

Pervading the earth and filling the heavens, silver mountains and iron walls stand firm; when the true command is fully raised, even the traces of empty space are erased. The crescent moon shines across horizontally to divide its function;
like falling stars and flashing lightning, it penetrates the Dragon Gate. It is said that the blind donkey knows no taboo; with a kick from his hoof, he turns out the old world.
He does not participate in the Chan of the Patriarchal Founder; he does not employ the "winter melon" seal. Holding the life-rope upside down, he alone upholds the command without transgression.
Neither heaven nor hell can contain him; he wanders at will through the Buddha-realm and the demon-palaces. While seeking a clear-water sluice-gate, he mistakenly entered the state of Chizheng.
Though he has two eyebrows, he does not recognize a single character. Before the pillar even conceived, his countenance was already like this.
Speaking of mind and nature, he brought three catties of hemp; urinating and defecating, he performed the Great Matter.
A-he-he! Do you see? In Jiangnan grows the black tree; in Jiangbei grows the heavenly creeper.
Holding his staff horizontally, he sits upon the flat rock; his nostrils pierce the heavens, his eyes bulge forth.
Pale mist enshrouds the ancient trees, a crescent moon hangs from the creeping vines. Entrust this to the brilliant Chan practitioner: examine and see through this old bhikṣu.

Swift as an arrow, straight as a bowstring. The patriarchs do not know where they have gone; the blind donkey continues to be lashed with a heavy whip.
Dwelling on Flying Tiger Peak, drinking cold spring water, he acts perversely and in reverse order, taking the head to be the tail. He beats the drum at the crossroads;

Even when exhaustively examined by those who have mastered the practice, everyone realizes that creating such an image is merely a semblance and not the reality; for empty space has no front or back, and a pillar grows roots while standing upright.

Leaning slightly to the side while pressing straight down with the hands clasped low; lifting the single staff alone while raising it high with a deep bow. Buddhas and demons are wiped from their traces; ordinary people and sages vanish without a mark.

Then, withdrawing his body, he returns to his original position and stands with palms joined, saying: "Fahui humbly awaits Your Majesty’s decree; I dare not act on my own authority."

Entering the ranks of the Māra king, dwelling in the forest of false views, yet practicing the bodhisattva path; manifesting the mind of a yakṣa, with a tongue trailing the ground—whom can recognize it?
With nostrils reaching to the heavens, there is nowhere to seek it.
The Great Way is vast and open; true emptiness leaves no trace. One sifts sand from within gold and discerns stone amidst jade.
Where the patch-robed monk acts, he breaks free from the cage; the tea kettle and the iron cauldron are not the same. With a single roar of the lion, the entire world is cleared of fox tracks.
Everywhere he speaks of Chan and speaks of the Way; for the sake of others, he enters the water and wades through the mud.
Having spent half his life establishing monasteries, he has now brought about his own ruin. Whether praised or reviled, Linji is nothing but a "white-handed thief"—a thief, a thief!
Yet even such a one is treated as if he were merely a piece of dried radish.

For the interment of Venerable Yuet-tang, he gazes into the mirror, withdrawing it entirely; its wondrous essence cannot be transmitted. As the stars shift and the constellations turn, it is as straight as a string.
Last night, having finished performing the Yunmen melody, he turns his head to see the springtime of the second month.
The Venerable Master Yuet-tang, Abbot of the Pure Compassion Monastery (Jingci) who entered perfect nirvana, relied upon Yuanwu in his youth and visited Xuefeng in his later years.
He unfurled the ancient sails at the head of Damei Creek and pierced the clear waves at the bottom of the Ocean of Wondrous Clarity.

Having repeatedly received imperial summons, he presided over renowned monasteries throughout the land. Cutting through iron and severing nails, chewing ginger and sipping vinegar, he upheld the wondrous Dharma for fifty years.
The Way! It is bent and borrowed, yet it provides a lifelong support. Establishing the Dharma banner, he picks it up alone and grasps it singularly.

When the time has arrived, he walks as soon as he finds the path. The life-force of the Buddhas and Patriarchs is like oil smeared on the feet; the orthodox lineage of Yunmen is like unraveling the thread of a sandal.
The heroic spirit of the patch-robed monks has withered away upon the Great Way; shattered and forgotten. Alas! The Great Mountain crumbles, the Sage has passed away.
The dark alleys are shrouded in gloom, and sentient beings have no refuge. Yet now, tigers crouch and dragons coil; monkeys wail and cranes lament.
The jade is buried in yellow earth, yet its fame shines brightly in the crimson heavens—this is indeed so. But I venture to ask the assembly: what is it?
The old man Yuet-tang’s phrase that does not reveal his wind-bone—could it be, "All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are laws of arising and ceasing.
When arising and ceasing have ceased, extinction is bliss"? Wrong, wrong! Ultimately, how is it? [He strikes the incense table once with his staff and says:

For the sake of the Zen practitioner, he holds up a torch as cold dew drips upon his dhyāna-robe. The northern wind scatters the withered leaves; casting off his hand, he walks toward that other shore. With a single step, he transcends all at once.
Every touch of the eye is Bodhi; it is but a speck of dust in the eyes of a patch-robed monk. A single blade of thatch after the fire—though one has a mouth, there is nowhere to clear it.
Only a Chan practitioner who has realized it deeply understands this moment: right here, beneath the mountain of ignorance, one immediately shatters the burden of self and personhood.
Immediately, he snapped it in two. "Go back! Go away! Life and death are not related. "Throughout past and present, one does not touch upon either the manifest or the subtle.

Listen attentively, listen attentively! Holding up a torch, he said: "All phenomena arise from conditions; when conditions cease, phenomena are extinguished.
My teacher, the Great Śramaṇa, always speaks thus."
For Old Long, the Elder, as he held the torch, there was no path through the four mountains;
he followed others away. A single point of reliance leaves one with doubt from beginning to end. When stagnant water meets the wind, waves arise.
Does Old Long have a time to turn himself around? Elder Long: Since you know how to turn yourself around, why were you unable to [do so] then?
Spitting out mist. Great assembly, if you were suddenly to be met by another who raises clouds and spits mist, where would you turn to evade it?

The willow by the bank leans with green like eyebrows; the petals of the pear-tree robe fly like snow. Zen student Mi, at such a time as this, what is it?
Red clouds disperse their brilliance as the moon sinks its luster; the golden-haired lion leaps from the dragon’s cave.
For Cao Yinlu, holding the torch for forty years:
how could this great dream not finally return? Departing and staying, he brushes away the eyes of fame and profit;
in life and death, he transcends the barriers of right and wrong. Alas! The autumn wind blows down the leaves; the autumn dew drips upon the lotuses.

This record of the oral instructions granted to Chan Master Fohai for his residence at Lingyin,
presented by the attendant-monk subject, has been carefully transcribed and submitted for imperial inspection.
On the seventh day of the third month in the seventh year of the Qiandao era, an imperial decree was issued:

on the eighth day at the hour of the horse (noon), the Emperor would mount his carriage to visit the Deshou Palace; upon his return, he commanded that the abbots of Lingyin and Jingshan enter together with him.

At Seondeokjeon Hall, he was summoned for an audience. The Master reported, saying: "On the thirtieth day of the first month, Your Majesty commanded me to have an audience, and I was granted the honor of beholding Your Majesty’s countenance.
On the seventh day of the second month, I was further graced with the gift of incense and tea. Thus he expressed his deep gratitude.
"Your Sacred Majesty’s grace is most profound and sincere. The Emperor granted him a seat, whereupon he expressed his thanks and took his place.
The Emperor said, "Lingyin and Jingshan are both great monasteries; I have frequently commanded my officials to select worthy persons to serve as abbots.
The Master replied, "It is a great honor that Your Majesty has not forgotten the entrustment of Vulture Peak, nor has cast aside those in humble robes. How can one such as I—"
[The Emperor] looked up in gratitude. The Emperor asked, "Last autumn there were floods; how is it this year? The Master replied, "The winter snows have fallen in season;

there will surely be signs of a bountiful harvest. The Emperor said, "I am deeply concerned that the common people may suffer from famine. The Master replied, "I, too, am concerned that the common folk will find it difficult to obtain food during the spring months. We rely [on the heavens for relief]."

Moved by Your Majesty’s sagely virtue, the two summer grains are now nearing ripeness and the price of rice has somewhat stabilized. Having secured capable men both at court and in the provinces, relief measures have already been implemented;
once the people are merely satiated, agricultural affairs will proceed in orderly fashion—all of which is the grace of Your Majesty’s creation and sustenance.
The Emperor said, "If we obtain another good harvest in the autumn, the common people will recover somewhat.
The Master replied, "Your Majesty takes the hearts of the common people as your own heart; since Your Holiness’s resolve is firm, it will surely follow that intention.
The Emperor said, "I have heard that in the past Huang Yanjie cited an ancient verse: 'The mind turns with the myriad objects; where it turns, it is truly profound.'"

"Because of this, one attains enjoyment. By responding to things with a vacant mind, as Jing-shan said: 'The void and luminous mind illuminates itself; there is no need for mental effort. The Master [Zhaozhou] reported:
'This is the *Xinxin Ming* (Inscription on Faith in Mind) by the Great Master, the Third Patriarch. It is specifically spoken for those who have attained realization.'"
The Emperor asked, "How is it so? The Master replied: "The Ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes discrimination. Simply do not harbor likes or dislikes, and all will be transparently clear.
A difference of a hair's breadth results in a gap as vast as heaven and earth. The Emperor was greatly pleased.

The Master requested, "I beg permission to transcribe a copy of this, along with the *Record of Iron-Tongue Hermitage* and the *Record of Previous and Subsequent Audiences*, to present to Your Majesty. The Emperor said:
"Excellent. He asked again, "Regarding 'drinking up the waters of the West River in a single gulp,' I have not yet understood this principle.
The Master replied, "It cannot be understood; where there is no path of meaning, it is right here and now. The Emperor said, "In a few more years, you must surely come to understand it.
The Master replied, "One need only take awakening as the standard within a single kṣaṇa. After the audience had lasted for some time, the Master addressed him, saying, "Your Servant..."
Fearing to weary the sagely hearing, he expressed his gratitude and descended from the hall.
